## Beyond Text: Preserving the Speaker's Voice Cross-language communication conveys not only information, but also the characteristics of a speaker's voice. Hy-SimulMT supports real-time voice cloning, preserving the original speaker's vocal characteristics while generating speech in the target language. The English-to-Chinese demo features three speakers. The model presents their distinct vocal characteristics, making it easier for listeners to tell who is speaking while following the translation. *The following two videos are offline replays provided for demonstration; their playback timing should not be interpreted as a live latency measurement.* ### English → Chinese Simultaneous Translation and Voice Cloning https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0a56fff0-8144-465d-83d0-7a014e914e07 [Watch the English → Chinese demo (1 minute 39 seconds)](assets/videos/en/en_zh_simultaneous_translation.mp4) ### Chinese → English Simultaneous Translation and Voice Cloning https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cf8b0814-1b1d-4c67-ac89-9d9433e94462 [Watch the Chinese → English demo (35 seconds)](assets/videos/en/zh_en_simultaneous_translation.mp4) From cross-language speeches to multi-speaker interviews, this capability opens up possibilities for more natural and more readily identifiable spoken communication. ## Continuing to Improve Through Real-World Feedback Simultaneous translation ultimately serves real communication. Beyond benchmark scores, we value professional interpreters' feedback on information delivery, response timing, and how natural the translated speech sounds. *The following statements are full English translations of the original Chinese remarks.* > Wang Weiwei, Vice Dean of the School of Interpreting and Translation Studies at Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, said: "In real-world evaluations, Tencent Hunyuan's simultaneous translation produces natural-sounding target-language speech and accurately conveys the main information in ordinary statements. To control latency, the system starts speaking first and makes corrections afterward; these corrections sound similar to an interpreter's self-corrections. This marks a new milestone in China's AI simultaneous interpreting capabilities (automatic speech translation, AST). As the technology continues to be refined, AI simultaneous interpreting is moving from 'assisting understanding' toward 'usable communication' in low-risk settings, providing important technical support for a new paradigm of human–machine collaboration in translation." > Professor Zhong Weihe, former President of Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, Rector of Macao Millennium College in Macao, China, former Executive Vice President of the Translators Association of China, and Chair of its Interpreting Committee, said: "Simultaneous interpreting is one of the most challenging areas of language services. Systematic evaluations show that Tencent Hunyuan's simultaneous translation model demonstrates notable capabilities in speech recognition stability, simultaneous translation response speed, and the quality of spoken translation output. These research and development achievements reflect the continued progress of AI simultaneous interpreting technology and provide strong technical support for bringing machine simultaneous interpreting into real-world settings." This feedback also points to a clear application path: helping AI simultaneous translation become useful first in appropriate low-risk settings, while continuing to improve through human–machine collaboration. From understanding the message to keeping pace with the speaker and delivering more natural speech, Hy-SimulMT aims to reduce the wait in cross-language communication and help information reach listeners more smoothly. --- ## Deploy inference > **Follow the [SimulInfer README](SimulInfer/README.md) for step-by-step installation, or use the one-command deployment below.** With `--install-server`, the command installs dependencies in isolated deployment environments. Running it again repeats the installation steps and may reinstall SimulInfer or change dependency versions in those environments. If you use a custom vLLM/CUDA environment or need control over dependency versions, follow the step-by-step guide or use the **Existing compatible vLLM environment** option below. **SimulInfer** provides a web page, audio file uploads, real-time WebSocket and optional TTS with input voice cloning. The deployed model determines whether source text is displayed; no output-mode selection is needed. ### vLLM Prepare a Linux machine with Python 3.12+, Git, an NVIDIA GPU with enough memory for the selected model, and a CUDA-compatible driver. For an existing model environment, use vLLM >=0.31 with `HYV3ForCausalLM` support and install `simulst`. Clone the project and enter the inference directory. Run the deployment commands below from `SimulInfer/`: ```bash git clone https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-SimulMT.git Hy-SimulMT cd Hy-SimulMT cd SimulInfer ``` **New environment — install dependencies and start both services:** ```bash bash deploy.sh --install-server --model tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-Interleave ``` For an accessible local checkpoint, replace the model ID: ```bash bash deploy.sh --install-server --model /path/to/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-Interleave ``` The command installs dependencies in separate environments, prepares the model, starts vLLM, then starts the web/API service. The first run downloads dependencies and, when using a Hugging Face ID, the model. Keep the command running. **Existing compatible vLLM environment:** ```bash /path/to/model-env/bin/python -m pip install --no-deps simulst bash deploy.sh --server-python /path/to/model-env/bin/python --model /path/to/model ``` This uses your existing model environment and creates a separate environment for the web service. For custom vLLM/CUDA builds, use this option. **Already running a model API:** ```bash bash deploy.sh --backend-url http://model-host:8800/v1 ``` This starts only SimulInfer. See the [model setup instructions](SimulInfer/README.md#manual-model-deployment) if the existing model needs its inference template prepared. #### Open and use Wait for `Ready: http://127.0.0.1:8080/`, then open that address on the server, or `http://SERVER_IP:8080/` from another machine. Select a translation direction, upload audio or start the microphone, then click **Stop and finish** when done. Remote microphone access requires HTTPS; use your HTTPS port-forwarding URL if available, including any `/proxy/8080/` prefix. Upload a file from the command line: ```bash curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8080/translate/stream \ -F direction=en-zh -F file=@audio.wav ``` Or open another terminal in `Hy-SimulMT/SimulInfer/` and use the installed client: ```bash .simulinfer/app-env/bin/simulinfer-client audio.wav --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 ``` When TTS is enabled in the deployment configuration, the same command also saves the returned speech to `outputs/translated.wav`. `/docs` provides API documentation. #### Configure and stop Defaults: web/API port **8080**, local model port **8800**. Files are saved under `SimulInfer/.simulinfer/`, including `config.toml`, `app.log` and `model.log` when a model is started. Press **Ctrl+C** to stop the services started by the command. An occupied port causes a startup error; select another port with `--port` or `--model-port`. For a saved deployment configuration: ```bash cp deploy.example.toml deploy.toml # Edit the model, GPU, ports and optional TTS connection. bash deploy.sh --config deploy.toml ``` Examples: ```bash bash deploy.sh --install-server --model /path/to/model --gpus 0 bash deploy.sh --install-server --model /path/to/model --gpus 0,1 --tensor-parallel-size 2 bash deploy.sh --backend-url http://model-host:8800/v1 --port 8081 --runtime-dir .simulinfer-alt ``` Use `SIMULINFER_PYTHON=python3.12` before the command if `python3` is not the Python version you want. Reuse the same deployment command to start it again. The detailed guide covers [installation and deployment options](SimulInfer/README.md), [configuration](SimulInfer/docs/CONFIGURATION.md), [audio clients](SimulInfer/docs/AUDIO_INPUT.en.md), and [TTS setup](SimulInfer/docs/TTS.en.md). ### llama.cpp We added architecture-specific support for Hy-SimulMT to llama.cpp to enable inference with GGUF models. We have submitted [PR #31198](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31198) to the llama.cpp repository. > This support has not yet been merged into the official llama.cpp repository. The PR currently supports inference through `llama-mtmd-cli`; `llama-server` support is planned as a follow-up. Before using the server deployment steps below, ensure that your llama.cpp version includes the required Hy-SimulMT server support. Use this option when an audio-capable llama.cpp server has already loaded your Hy-SimulMT GGUF model on port **8080**. In a Python 3.11+ environment, run the following from the repository root: ```bash cd SimulInfer python -m pip install . export MODEL=/path/to/hymt-A3b-tgt_only-1019-Q8_0.gguf MODEL_TYPE=target_only python serve_llamacpp.py ``` Replace `MODEL` with your own GGUF path, exactly as loaded by the llama.cpp server. Use `MODEL_TYPE=target_only` for a translation-only model, or `source_target` for a model that outputs both source text and translation. For `serve_llamacpp.py`, open **http://127.0.0.1:8094/** for the web page. This is the bridge web/API port; **8080** is the default llama.cpp model port. The separate `deploy.sh` / `simulinfer` launch path defaults to web/API port **8080**. For the llama.cpp bridge, file uploads and WebSocket use `/translate/stream` and `/translate/ws` on port **8094**. The script connects to `http://127.0.0.1:8080` by default; set `LLAMA_URL` for a different model server and `PORT` for a different web/API port. For remote microphone access, use an HTTPS port-forwarding address. ### SGLang-Omni [X-post](https://x.com/sgl_project/status/2114995700010516510?s=20) [SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni) is a multi-stage serving runtime that serves Hy-SimulMT through OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoints and a realtime WebSocket. It covers this checkpoint (`Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B`, BF16, translation-only output). It returns translated text only: speech output and voice cloning require a separate TTS service, and the FP8, GGUF and Interleave checkpoints are not covered by this integration. Requirements: Linux with an NVIDIA GPU and a CUDA driver. The BF16 weights occupy about 57 GiB before KV cache and runtime allocations, so a single H200 is sufficient. Docker is recommended, because UCX, flash-attn, SGLang and CUDA are prebuilt: ```bash docker run -it \ --shm-size 32g \ --gpus all \ --ipc host \ --network host \ --privileged \ hongccc/sglang-omni:dev \ /bin/zsh ``` Inside the container, install `sglang-omni`: ```bash git clone https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni.git cd sglang-omni pip install --upgrade pip pip install uv uv venv .venv -p 3.12 source .venv/bin/activate uv pip install --prerelease=allow -v -e . ``` Start the server: ```bash sgl-omni serve \ --model-path tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B \ --mem-fraction-static 0.75 \ --enable-realtime \ --port 8000 ``` Decode CUDA graphs are enabled and Torch compilation is disabled by default. `--enable-realtime` is only required for the streaming WebSocket below. The web/API port here is **8000**, not the 8080 used by SimulInfer. For Chinese speech to English text: ```bash curl http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/translations \ -F file=@chinese.wav \ -F language=zh \ -F response_format=json ``` For English speech to Chinese text: ```bash curl http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/transcriptions \ -F file=@english.wav \ -F language=en \ -F response_format=json ``` `language` is the source language (`zh` or `en`); pass it explicitly, because this checkpoint provides no language-detection tokens. Omitting it defaults to Chinese-to-English. Each request accepts one file of at most 30 seconds; longer audio is rejected rather than truncated. Add `-F stream=true` to either endpoint to receive `transcript.text.delta` SSE events followed by the authoritative `transcript.text.done`. Live audio uses `/v1/realtime?intent=transcription` (requires `--enable-realtime`) with mono PCM16 at 16 kHz: 1. Send `session.update` with `session.language` set to the source language (`zh` or `en`). 2. Send base64 PCM chunks with `input_audio_buffer.append`. 3. Receive `transcription.segment` translation hypotheses, refreshed every 1.6 seconds. 4. Send `input_audio_buffer.commit` to finish a segment, or `transcription.done` to finish input. Each partial request keeps earlier audio turns and their translations as context; the final hypothesis re-translates the complete segment and can revise earlier partial translations. The runtime starts a fresh translation context after 30 seconds. This path does not reproduce SimulInfer's VAD and recovery heuristics. See the [Hy-SimulMT cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/hy_simulmt.html) for request parameters, streaming behavior, reference validation against Transformers, and measured latency (up to 6.5x faster than Transformers on H200 at batch size one). ## Train — SimulTrain **SimulTrain** continues training from a downloaded Hy-SimulMT checkpoint. Configure model paths, datasets, GPUs and output directories in `SimulTrain/.env`. From the repository root: ```bash cd SimulTrain ``` See the [training guide](SimulTrain/README.md) or [Simplified Chinese version](SimulTrain/README.zh-CN.md) for environment setup, data formats, and training commands. Use a separate Python environment for training. ## Contributors Mao Zheng, Bo Lv, Mingrui Sun, Zheng Li, Fangxu Liu, Tao Chen, Bingxin Qu, Shan Yang, rickkan, Steve Yves, Rilin Chen, Longsha Zhou, Guanghua Yu, Decheng Wu, Hongyu Li ## Citing Hy-SimulMT If you find Hy-SimulMT useful, please cite: ```bibtex @misc{hy_simulmt, title = {Hy-SimulMT：A Low-Latency, High-Quality Model for Real-Time Simultaneous Translation}, author = {Mao Zheng and Bo Lv and Mingrui Sun and Zheng Li and Fangxu Liu and Tao Chen and Bingxin Qu}, year = {2026}, month = oct, url = {https://hy.tencent.com/model/open-source-model/detail?id=hy-simulmt} } ``` ## Contact Us If you would like to leave a message for our research and product teams, please contact the Tencent Hunyuan LLM team at [hunyuan_opensource@tencent.com](mailto:hunyuan_opensource@tencent.com).

The model presents their distinct vocal characteristics, making it easier for listeners to tell who is speaking while following the translation. *The following two videos are offline replays provided for demonstration; their playback timing should not be interpreted as a live latency measurement.* ### English → Chinese Simultaneous Translation and Voice Cloning [Watch the English → Chinese demo (1 minute 39 seconds)](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B/resolve/main/assets/videos/en/en_zh_simultaneous_translation.mp4) ### Chinese → English Simultaneous Translation and Voice Cloning [Watch the Chinese → English demo (35 seconds)](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B/resolve/main/assets/videos/en/zh_en_simultaneous_translation.mp4) From cross-language speeches to multi-speaker interviews, this capability opens up possibilities for more natural and more readily identifiable spoken communication. ## Continuing to Improve Through Real-World Feedback Simultaneous translation ultimately serves real communication. Beyond benchmark scores, we value professional interpreters' feedback on information delivery, response timing, and how natural the translated speech sounds. *The following statements are full English translations of the original Chinese remarks.* > Wang Weiwei, Vice Dean of the School of Interpreting and Translation Studies at Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, said: "In real-world evaluations, Tencent Hunyuan's simultaneous translation produces natural-sounding target-language speech and accurately conveys the main information in ordinary statements. To control latency, the system starts speaking first and makes corrections afterward; these corrections sound similar to an interpreter's self-corrections. This marks a new milestone in China's AI simultaneous interpreting capabilities (automatic speech translation, AST). As the technology continues to be refined, AI simultaneous interpreting is moving from 'assisting understanding' toward 'usable communication' in low-risk settings, providing important technical support for a new paradigm of human–machine collaboration in translation." > Professor Zhong Weihe, former President of Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, Rector of Macao Millennium College in Macao, China, former Executive Vice President of the Translators Association of China, and Chair of its Interpreting Committee, said: "Simultaneous interpreting is one of the most challenging areas of language services. Systematic evaluations show that Tencent Hunyuan's simultaneous translation model demonstrates notable capabilities in speech recognition stability, simultaneous translation response speed, and the quality of spoken translation output. These research and development achievements reflect the continued progress of AI simultaneous interpreting technology and provide strong technical support for bringing machine simultaneous interpreting into real-world settings." This feedback also points to a clear application path: helping AI simultaneous translation become useful first in appropriate low-risk settings, while continuing to improve through human–machine collaboration. Professional interpreters remain important in scenarios requiring strict accountability, expert review, or high-stakes decisions. ## Model Links | Model | Description | Download | | --- | --- | --- | | Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B | Hunyuan simultaneous translation model, translation-only output | [Model](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B) | | Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-FP8 | Hunyuan simultaneous translation model, translation-only output, FP8 quantization | [Model](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-FP8) | | Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-GGUF | Hunyuan simultaneous translation model, translation-only output, GGUF format | [Model](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-GGUF) | | Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-Interleave | Hunyuan simultaneous translation model, source text and translation output | [Model](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-Interleave) | | Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-Interleave-FP8 | Hunyuan simultaneous translation model, source text and translation output, FP8 quantization | [Model](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-Interleave-FP8) | | Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-Interleave-GGUF | Hunyuan simultaneous translation model, source text and translation output, GGUF format | [Model](https://huggingface.co/tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-Interleave-GGUF) | Model collections: [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/collections/tencent/hy-simulmt) | [ModelScope](https://www.modelscope.cn/collections/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-SimulMT). Try Hy-SimulMT in the **Hy Translate App**. Download QR codes are available in the [Introduction](#introduction) above. From understanding the message to keeping pace with the speaker and delivering more natural speech, Hy-SimulMT aims to reduce the wait in cross-language communication and help information reach listeners more smoothly. --- ## Deploy inference > **Follow the [SimulInfer README](https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-SimulMT/blob/main/SimulInfer/README.md) for step-by-step installation, or use the one-command deployment below.** With `--install-server`, the command installs dependencies in isolated deployment environments. Running it again repeats the installation steps and may reinstall SimulInfer or change dependency versions in those environments. If you use a custom vLLM/CUDA environment or need control over dependency versions, follow the step-by-step guide or use the **Existing compatible vLLM environment** option below. **SimulInfer** provides a web page, audio file uploads, real-time WebSocket and optional TTS with input voice cloning. The deployed model determines whether source text is displayed; no output-mode selection is needed. ### vLLM Prepare a Linux machine with Python 3.12+, Git, an NVIDIA GPU with enough memory for the selected model, and a CUDA-compatible driver. For an existing model environment, use vLLM >=0.31 with `HYV3ForCausalLM` support and install `simulst`. Clone the project and enter the inference directory. Run the deployment commands below from `SimulInfer/`: ```bash git clone https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-SimulMT.git Hy-SimulMT cd Hy-SimulMT cd SimulInfer ``` **New environment — install dependencies and start both services:** ```bash bash deploy.sh --install-server --model tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-Interleave ``` For an accessible local checkpoint, replace the model ID: ```bash bash deploy.sh --install-server --model /path/to/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B-Interleave ``` The command installs dependencies in separate environments, prepares the model, starts vLLM, then starts the web/API service. The first run downloads dependencies and, when using a Hugging Face ID, the model. Keep the command running. **Existing compatible vLLM environment:** ```bash /path/to/model-env/bin/python -m pip install --no-deps simulst bash deploy.sh --server-python /path/to/model-env/bin/python --model /path/to/model ``` This uses your existing model environment and creates a separate environment for the web service. For custom vLLM/CUDA builds, use this option. **Already running a model API:** ```bash bash deploy.sh --backend-url http://model-host:8800/v1 ``` This starts only SimulInfer. See the [model setup instructions](https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-SimulMT/blob/main/SimulInfer/README.md#manual-model-deployment) if the existing model needs its inference template prepared. #### Open and use Wait for `Ready: http://127.0.0.1:8080/`, then open that address on the server, or `http://SERVER_IP:8080/` from another machine. Select a translation direction, upload audio or start the microphone, then click **Stop and finish** when done. Remote microphone access requires HTTPS; use your HTTPS port-forwarding URL if available, including any `/proxy/8080/` prefix. Upload a file from the command line: ```bash curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8080/translate/stream \ -F direction=en-zh -F file=@audio.wav ``` Or open another terminal in `Hy-SimulMT/SimulInfer/` and use the installed client: ```bash .simulinfer/app-env/bin/simulinfer-client audio.wav --url http://127.0.0.1:8080 ``` When TTS is enabled in the deployment configuration, the same command also saves the returned speech to `outputs/translated.wav`. `/docs` provides API documentation. #### Configure and stop Defaults: web/API port **8080**, local model port **8800**. Files are saved under `SimulInfer/.simulinfer/`, including `config.toml`, `app.log` and `model.log` when a model is started. Press **Ctrl+C** to stop the services started by the command. An occupied port causes a startup error; select another port with `--port` or `--model-port`. For a saved deployment configuration: ```bash cp deploy.example.toml deploy.toml # Edit the model, GPU, ports and optional TTS connection. bash deploy.sh --config deploy.toml ``` Examples: ```bash bash deploy.sh --install-server --model /path/to/model --gpus 0 bash deploy.sh --install-server --model /path/to/model --gpus 0,1 --tensor-parallel-size 2 bash deploy.sh --backend-url http://model-host:8800/v1 --port 8081 --runtime-dir .simulinfer-alt ``` Use `SIMULINFER_PYTHON=python3.12` before the command if `python3` is not the Python version you want. Reuse the same deployment command to start it again. The detailed guide covers [installation and deployment options](https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-SimulMT/blob/main/SimulInfer/README.md), [configuration](https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-SimulMT/blob/main/SimulInfer/docs/CONFIGURATION.md), [audio clients](https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-SimulMT/blob/main/SimulInfer/docs/AUDIO_INPUT.en.md), and [TTS setup](https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-SimulMT/blob/main/SimulInfer/docs/TTS.en.md). ### llama.cpp We added architecture-specific support for Hy-SimulMT to llama.cpp to enable inference with GGUF models. We have submitted [PR #31198](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31198) to the llama.cpp repository. > This support has not yet been merged into the official llama.cpp repository. The PR currently supports inference through `llama-mtmd-cli`; `llama-server` support is planned as a follow-up. Before using the server deployment steps below, ensure that your llama.cpp version includes the required Hy-SimulMT server support. Use this option when an audio-capable llama.cpp server has already loaded your Hy-SimulMT GGUF model on port **8080**. In a Python 3.11+ environment, run the following from the repository root: ```bash cd SimulInfer python -m pip install . export MODEL=/path/to/hymt-A3b-tgt_only-1019-Q8_0.gguf MODEL_TYPE=target_only python serve_llamacpp.py ``` Replace `MODEL` with your own GGUF path, exactly as loaded by the llama.cpp server. Use `MODEL_TYPE=target_only` for a translation-only model, or `source_target` for a model that outputs both source text and translation. For `serve_llamacpp.py`, open **http://127.0.0.1:8094/** for the web page. This is the bridge web/API port; **8080** is the default llama.cpp model port. The separate `deploy.sh` / `simulinfer` launch path defaults to web/API port **8080**. For the llama.cpp bridge, file uploads and WebSocket use `/translate/stream` and `/translate/ws` on port **8094**. The script connects to `http://127.0.0.1:8080` by default; set `LLAMA_URL` for a different model server and `PORT` for a different web/API port. For remote microphone access, use an HTTPS port-forwarding address. ### SGLang-Omni [X-post](https://x.com/sgl_project/status/2114995700010516510?s=20) [SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni) is a multi-stage serving runtime that serves Hy-SimulMT through OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoints and a realtime WebSocket. It covers this checkpoint (`Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B`, BF16, translation-only output). It returns translated text only: speech output and voice cloning require a separate TTS service, and the FP8, GGUF and Interleave checkpoints are not covered by this integration. Requirements: Linux with an NVIDIA GPU and a CUDA driver. The BF16 weights occupy about 57 GiB before KV cache and runtime allocations, so a single H200 is sufficient. Docker is recommended, because UCX, flash-attn, SGLang and CUDA are prebuilt: ```bash docker run -it \ --shm-size 32g \ --gpus all \ --ipc host \ --network host \ --privileged \ hongccc/sglang-omni:dev \ /bin/zsh ``` Inside the container, install `sglang-omni`: ```bash git clone https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni.git cd sglang-omni pip install --upgrade pip pip install uv uv venv .venv -p 3.12 source .venv/bin/activate uv pip install --prerelease=allow -v -e . ``` Start the server: ```bash sgl-omni serve \ --model-path tencent/Hy-SimulMT-30B-A3B \ --mem-fraction-static 0.75 \ --enable-realtime \ --port 8000 ``` Decode CUDA graphs are enabled and Torch compilation is disabled by default. `--enable-realtime` is only required for the streaming WebSocket below. The web/API port here is **8000**, not the 8080 used by SimulInfer. For Chinese speech to English text: ```bash curl http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/translations \ -F file=@chinese.wav \ -F language=zh \ -F response_format=json ``` For English speech to Chinese text: ```bash curl http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/transcriptions \ -F file=@english.wav \ -F language=en \ -F response_format=json ``` `language` is the source language (`zh` or `en`); pass it explicitly, because this checkpoint provides no language-detection tokens. Omitting it defaults to Chinese-to-English. Each request accepts one file of at most 30 seconds; longer audio is rejected rather than truncated. Add `-F stream=true` to either endpoint to receive `transcript.text.delta` SSE events followed by the authoritative `transcript.text.done`. Live audio uses `/v1/realtime?intent=transcription` (requires `--enable-realtime`) with mono PCM16 at 16 kHz: 1. Send `session.update` with `session.language` set to the source language (`zh` or `en`). 2. Send base64 PCM chunks with `input_audio_buffer.append`. 3. Receive `transcription.segment` translation hypotheses, refreshed every 1.6 seconds. 4. Send `input_audio_buffer.commit` to finish a segment, or `transcription.done` to finish input. Each partial request keeps earlier audio turns and their translations as context; the final hypothesis re-translates the complete segment and can revise earlier partial translations. The runtime starts a fresh translation context after 30 seconds. This path does not reproduce SimulInfer's VAD and recovery heuristics. See the [Hy-SimulMT cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/hy_simulmt.html) for request parameters, streaming behavior, reference validation against Transformers, and measured latency (up to 6.5x faster than Transformers on H200 at batch size one). ## Train — SimulTrain **SimulTrain** continues training from a downloaded Hy-SimulMT checkpoint. Configure model paths, datasets, GPUs and output directories in `SimulTrain/.env`. From the repository root: ```bash cd SimulTrain ``` See the [training guide](https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-SimulMT/blob/main/SimulTrain/README.md) or [Simplified Chinese version](https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-SimulMT/blob/main/SimulTrain/README.zh-CN.md) for environment setup, data formats, and training commands. Use a separate Python environment for training. ## Contributors Mao Zheng, Bo Lv, Mingrui Sun, Zheng Li, Fangxu Liu, Tao Chen, Bingxin Qu, Shan Yang, rickkan, Steve Yves, Rilin Chen, Longsha Zhou, Guanghua Yu, Decheng Wu, Hongyu Li ## Citing Hy-SimulMT If you find Hy-SimulMT useful, please cite: ```bibtex @misc{hy_simulmt, title = {Hy-SimulMT：A Low-Latency, High-Quality Model for Real-Time Simultaneous Translation}, author = {Mao Zheng and Bo Lv and Mingrui Sun and Zheng Li and Fangxu Liu and Tao Chen and Bingxin Qu}, year = {2026}, month = oct, url = {https://hy.tencent.com/model/open-source-model/detail?id=hy-simulmt} } ``` ## Contact Us If you would like to leave a message for our research and product teams, please contact the Tencent Hunyuan LLM team at [hunyuan_opensource@tencent.com](mailto:hunyuan_opensource@tencent.com).

Claude Code Game Studios

Turn a single Claude Code session into a full game development studio.
49 agents. 74 skills. One coordinated AI team.

--- ## Why This Exists Building a game solo with AI is powerful — but a single chat session has no structure. No one stops you from hardcoding magic numbers, skipping design docs, or writing spaghetti code. There's no QA pass, no design review, no one asking "does this actually fit the game's vision?" **Claude Code Game Studios** solves this by giving your AI session the structure of a real studio. Instead of one general-purpose assistant, you get 49 specialized agents organized into a studio hierarchy — directors who guard the vision, department leads who own their domains, and specialists who do the hands-on work. Each agent has defined responsibilities, escalation paths, and quality gates. The result: you still make every decision, but now you have a team that asks the right questions, catches mistakes early, and keeps your project organized from first brainstorm to launch. --- ## Table of Contents - [What's Included](#whats-included) - [Studio Hierarchy](#studio-hierarchy) - [Slash Commands](#slash-commands) - [Does it produce games, or documents?](#does-it-produce-games-or-documents) - [Getting Started](#getting-started) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Upgrading](#upgrading) - [Project Structure](#project-structure) - [How It Works](#how-it-works) - [Design Philosophy](#design-philosophy) - [Customization](#customization) - [Platform Support](#platform-support) - [Community](#community) - [Supporting This Project](#supporting-this-project) - [License](#license) --- ## What's Included | Category | Count | Description | |----------|-------|-------------| | **Agents** | 49 | Specialized subagents across design, programming, art, audio, narrative, QA, and production | | **Skills** | 74 | Slash commands for every workflow phase (`/start`, `/design-system`, `/create-epics`, `/create-stories`, `/dev-story`, `/story-done`, etc.) | | **Hooks** | 15 | Automated validation on commits, pushes, asset changes, design-doc reads, writes and registries, session lifecycle, agent audit trail, and gap detection | | **Rules** | 14 | Path-scoped coding standards enforced when editing gameplay, engine, AI, UI, network code, scene and asset files, and more | | **Templates** | 62 | Document templates for GDDs, UX specs, ADRs, sprint plans, HUD design, accessibility, and more | ## Studio Hierarchy Agents are organized into three tiers, matching how real studios operate: ``` Tier 1 — Directors creative-director technical-director producer Tier 2 — Department Leads game-designer lead-programmer art-director audio-director narrative-director qa-lead release-manager localization-lead Tier 3 — Specialists gameplay-programmer engine-programmer ai-programmer network-programmer tools-programmer ui-programmer systems-designer level-designer economy-designer technical-artist sound-designer writer world-builder ux-designer prototyper performance-analyst devops-engineer analytics-engineer security-engineer qa-tester accessibility-specialist live-ops-designer community-manager ``` Each agent declares a model in its frontmatter: the three directors ask for Opus, `lead-programmer` and fifteen specialists name Sonnet, and the remaining thirty **inherit your session's model**. Treat the tiers as seniority of role, not as a billing plan — most of the studio runs on whatever model you are already using. ### Engine Specialists The template includes agent sets for all three major engines. Use the set that matches your project: | Engine | Lead Agent | Sub-Specialists | |--------|-----------|-----------------| | **Godot 4** | `godot-specialist` | GDScript, Shaders, GDExtension | | **Unity** | `unity-specialist` | DOTS/ECS, Shaders/VFX, Addressables, UI Toolkit | | **Unreal Engine 5** | `unreal-specialist` | GAS, Blueprints, Replication, UMG/CommonUI | ## Slash Commands Type `/` in Claude Code to access all 74 skills: **Onboarding & Navigation** `/start` `/help` `/project-stage-detect` `/setup-engine` `/adopt` `/settings` **Game Design** `/brainstorm` `/map-systems` `/design-system` `/quick-design` `/review-all-gdds` `/propagate-design-change` **Art & Assets** `/art-bible` `/asset-spec` `/asset-audit` **UX & Interface Design** `/ux-design` `/ux-review` **Architecture** `/create-architecture` `/architecture-decision` `/architecture-review` `/create-control-manifest` **Stories & Sprints** `/create-epics` `/create-stories` `/dev-story` `/sprint-plan` `/sprint-status` `/story-readiness` `/story-done` `/estimate` **Reviews & Analysis** `/design-review` `/code-review` `/balance-check` `/content-audit` `/scope-check` `/perf-profile` `/tech-debt` `/gate-check` `/consistency-check` `/security-audit` **QA & Testing** `/qa-plan` `/smoke-check` `/soak-test` `/regression-suite` `/test-setup` `/test-helpers` `/test-evidence-review` `/test-flakiness` `/skill-test` `/skill-improve` **Production** `/milestone-review` `/retrospective` `/bug-report` `/bug-triage` `/reverse-document` `/playtest-report` **Release** `/release-checklist` `/launch-checklist` `/changelog` `/patch-notes` `/hotfix` `/day-one-patch` **Creative & Content** `/prototype` `/vertical-slice` `/onboard` `/localize` **Team Orchestration** (coordinate multiple agents on a single feature) `/team-combat` `/team-narrative` `/team-ui` `/team-release` `/team-polish` `/team-audio` `/team-level` `/team-live-ops` `/team-qa` ## Does it produce games, or documents? A fair question, and the answer is a measurement rather than a sample project. Four games were built from one brief at different `modes.rigor` levels and the documents each wrote **before its first line of game code** were counted: | `modes.rigor` | Docs before first line of game code | Time | |---|---:|---:| | `minimal` | **1** (the one-page brief) | 0 min | | `standard` | 30 | 58 min | All of them produced a running, tested game. Two blind reviewers and a human playtest then ranked the `standard` build **last** — the extra 29 documents bought traceability, not a better game. ### It runs the game and looks at it The measurement above is about cost. The other half is whether the thing works, and for a game that means someone has to *look* at it — a passing test says nothing about a menu drawn off-screen. So a story that changes anything the player sees is not closed until the game has been launched, observed, and a screenshot retained in `production/qa/evidence/`. A parse check is not a run. This holds at every rigor level, including `minimal`, where automated tests are waived but the look is not. The games themselves are deliberately **not** shipped here: this is a template you clone to start your own project, and somebody else's game in your repo is clutter, not evidence. ## Getting Started ### Prerequisites - [Git](https://git-scm.com/) - [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup) — the native installer is recommended (`npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` also works, on Node.js 22+) - [Python 3](https://www.python.org/) — reads `project.yaml` for every skill and hook; without it every setting silently falls back to its default - Bash — runs every hook; built into macOS and Linux, and on Windows it comes with [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win) - **Recommended**: [jq](https://jqlang.github.io/jq/) (for hook validation) Hooks fail gracefully if optional tools are missing — you just lose validation — with one deliberate exception: a commit that stages data JSON is blocked when there is no Python to validate it. ### Setup 1. **Clone or use as template**: ```bash git clone https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios.git my-game cd my-game ``` 2. **Open Claude Code in the project's root folder** (the one holding `CLAUDE.md` and `project.yaml`) and start a session: ```bash claude ``` Starting it in a subfolder such as `src/` skips the project's hooks, deny rules and ask-first permission mode. 3. **Run `/start`** — the system asks where you are (no idea, vague concept, clear design, existing work) and guides you to the right workflow. No assumptions. Or jump directly to a specific skill if you already know what you need: - `/brainstorm` — explore game ideas from scratch - `/setup-engine godot 4.7` — configure your engine if you already know - `/project-stage-detect` — analyze an existing project ## Configuration `project.yaml` at the repo root is the single source of truth for how the studio behaves on your project — engine, naming conventions, and a `modes` block that controls how much process every skill enforces. `/start` writes it for you; you rarely need to hand-edit it. The one question that matters most is **`modes.rigor`** — `minimal`, `standard`, or `full`. It's a single front door over six separate knobs (`workflow` — which GDD sections are required, `docs.density`, `qa.level`, `story_granularity`, `review_mode` — how many director agents review your work, and `team.size`), so `/start` asks it once instead of six times: - **`minimal`** (default) — jam-game speed. No GDDs required, terse docs, minimal QA evidence, solo review. `/start` → `/setup-engine` → `/brainstorm` (a one-page brief) → `/create-stories` → `/dev-story` ↔ `/story-done`. - **`standard`** — 5 required GDD sections, balanced doc depth, standard QA evidence, lean review. - **`full`** — all 8 GDD sections, thorough docs, full QA evidence on every story type, full director review. `minimal` is the default because the heavier tier costs more to reach working code without producing a better result, and gives nothing back when someone new picks the project up. Raise it in one `/settings` call when your project grows — `/help` and `/gate-check` will suggest it when they see the signs. Two escape hatches keep one setting from being a blunt instrument. **`system_overrides`** holds a single system to a higher standard than the rest of the project — your combat system gets the full treatment while everything else stays light. **`testing.strict`** sets, per test type (logic, integration, visual, UI, config), whether missing evidence blocks a story or merely warns. Any of the six underlying knobs can still be set individually if you want a mix (e.g. `workflow: full` with `docs.density: terse` — comprehensive but compact). Two of them — `review_mode` (`full` / `lean` / `solo`) and `team.size` — are also **personal**: rigor sets the team-wide default, but you can override them per-developer in a gitignored `project.local.yaml` without touching the shared config. `modes.automation` (how often the AI pauses to ask before it acts) sits outside rigor and is likewise personally overridable. View or change any setting with the `/settings` skill: ``` /settings # view effective config /settings modes.review_mode # view one setting /settings modes.rigor=full # write to project.yaml (team-wide) /settings --local modes.review_mode=solo # write to project.local.yaml (just you) ``` Full schema and per-setting behavior: `.claude/docs/effects-map.md`. ## Upgrading Already using an older version of this template? See [UPGRADING.md](UPGRADING.md) for step-by-step migration instructions, a breakdown of what changed between versions, and which files are safe to overwrite vs. which need a manual merge. ## Project Structure ``` CLAUDE.md # Master configuration .claude/ settings.json # Hooks, permissions, safety rules agents/ # 49 agent definitions (markdown + YAML frontmatter) skills/ # 74 slash commands (subdirectory per skill) hooks/ # 18 scripts (bash) — 15 event hooks, two helpers they # source (yaml-helper.sh, update-check.sh), and one # opt-in diagnostic you wire yourself rules/ # 14 path-scoped coding standards statusline.sh # Status line script (context%, model, stage, epic breadcrumb) docs/ workflow-catalog.yaml # 7-phase pipeline definition (read by /help) templates/ # 62 document templates (+ per-section guidance) src/ # Game source code (Godot). The code root is # ENGINE-SPECIFIC: Unity compiles only # Assets/, Unreal builds from Source// assets/ # Art, audio, VFX, shaders, data files design/ # GDDs, narrative docs, level designs docs/ # Technical documentation and ADRs tests/ # Test suites (unit, integration, performance, playtest) tools/ # Build and pipeline tools prototypes/ # Throwaway prototypes (isolated from src/) production/ # Sprint plans, milestones, release tracking studio-tests/ # QA for the skills and agents themselves — see below ``` ### Testing your customizations CCGS is a template you are meant to edit. `studio-tests/` is how you check that an edited or newly written skill still holds up — a catalog of all 74 skills and 49 agents, per-category quality rubrics, behavioral specs, and templates for writing specs of your own. ``` /skill-test static [name] # structural linter — 7 compliance checks /skill-test category [name] # category-specific quality rubric /skill-test spec [name] # behavioral spec assertions /skill-test audit # coverage report across skills and agents /skill-improve [name] # test-fix-retest loop; keeps or reverts on score change ``` It tests the *framework*, never your game — game tests live in `tests/`. ## How It Works ### Agent Coordination Agents follow a structured delegation model: 1. **Vertical delegation** — directors delegate to leads, leads delegate to specialists 2. **Horizontal consultation** — same-tier agents can consult each other but can't make binding cross-domain decisions 3. **Conflict resolution** — disagreements escalate up to the shared parent (`creative-director` for design, `technical-director` for technical) 4. **Change propagation** — cross-department changes are coordinated by `producer` 5. **Domain boundaries** — agents don't modify files outside their domain without explicit delegation ### Collaborative, Not Autonomous This is **not** an auto-pilot system. Every agent follows a strict collaboration protocol: 1. **Ask** — agents ask questions before proposing solutions 2. **Present options** — agents show 2-4 options with pros/cons 3. **You decide** — the user always makes the call 4. **Draft** — agents show work before finalizing 5. **Approve** — nothing gets written without your sign-off You stay in control. The agents provide structure and expertise, not autonomy. That is how a terminal session started at the project root behaves out of the box. The `guided` and `autonomous` automation settings, and Claude Code's own auto mode, trade some of these prompts for speed; see [setup-requirements.md](.claude/docs/setup-requirements.md) for the routes into auto mode. ### Automated Safety **Hooks** run automatically on every session: | Hook | Trigger | What It Does | |------|---------|--------------| | `validate-commit.sh` | PreToolUse (Bash, PowerShell) | Checks for hardcoded values, TODO format, JSON validity, design doc sections — exits early if the command is not `git commit` | | `validate-push.sh` | PreToolUse (Bash, PowerShell) | Warns on pushes to protected branches, and on `git tag`, `git merge`, `gh release`, `butler push` and `steamcmd +run_app_build` — exits early for any other command | | `validate-read.sh` | PreToolUse (Read) | Refuses a whole-file read of a design doc over 40 KB and answers with its headings, so the retry reads one section (`features.read_guard`) | | `validate-write.sh` | PreToolUse (Write/Edit) | Warns, never blocks, when a write would break a rule the skills state: a file they never overwrite, the config guard, the prototype boundary, a localization freeze | | `validate-registry.sh` | PreToolUse (Write/Edit) | Warns when a write to the entity or TR-ID registry would delete or renumber an entry, or set a status its header does not list | | `validate-assets.sh` | PostToolUse (Write/Edit) | Checks data-file JSON under `assets/`, `Assets/` or `Content/`, and asset naming in Godot's `assets/` only — exits early if the file is under none of them | | `session-start.sh` | Session open | Shows current branch and recent commits for orientation | | `detect-gaps.sh` | Session open | Detects fresh projects (suggests `/start`) and missing design docs when code or prototypes exist | | `pre-compact.sh` | Before compaction | Logs the compaction (its output does not reach Claude — `session-start.sh` restores context afterwards) | | `notify.sh` | Permission prompt, or idle about a minute | Shows Windows toast notification via PowerShell | | `session-stop.sh` | Every response end, in the background | Archives `active.md` to session log and records git activity | | `log-agent.sh` | Agent spawned | Audit trail start — logs subagent invocation | | `log-agent-stop.sh` | Agent stops | Audit trail stop — completes subagent record | | `validate-agent-artifact.sh` | Agent stops | Warns when a subagent stops without writing the file its brief named | | `validate-skill-change.sh` | PostToolUse (Write/Edit) | Advises running `/skill-test` after any `.claude/skills/` change | > **Note**: `validate-commit.sh`, `validate-push.sh`, `validate-read.sh`, `validate-write.sh`, `validate-registry.sh`, `validate-assets.sh` and `validate-skill-change.sh` fire on every Bash, PowerShell, Read, Write or Edit tool call and exit immediately (exit 0) when the command or file path is not relevant. This is normal hook behavior — not a performance concern. **Permission rules** in `settings.json` auto-allow test runs and block dangerous operations (force push, `rm -rf`, reading `.env` files) in both the Bash and PowerShell tools. Read-only commands such as `git status`, `git log` and `ls` need no rule: Claude Code runs them without asking. The `git` rules match anywhere after `git`, so a git command whose text only mentions `push` followed later by ` +` or ` -f`, `clean` followed by ` -f`, or `reset` followed by `--hard` — a commit message such as `git commit -m "push + pull"` included — is denied too: reword the message. ### Path-Scoped Rules Coding standards are automatically enforced based on file location. The paths below are Godot's. Each rule also matches the Unity and Unreal layouts: the code rules match C# under `Assets/**/Gameplay/` and C++ under `Source/**/Gameplay/` (and `Core`, `AI`, `Networking`, `UI`), data matches JSON under `Assets/**/Data/` and `Content/**/Data/`, shaders match by file type, and tests match C# under `Assets/Tests/` and C++ under `Source/**/Tests/`. | Path | Enforces | |------|----------| | `src/gameplay/**` | Data-driven values, delta time usage, no UI references | | `src/core/**` | Zero allocations in hot paths, thread safety, API stability | | `src/ai/**` | Performance budgets, debuggability, data-driven parameters | | `src/networking/**` | Server-authoritative, versioned messages, security | | `src/ui/**` | No game state ownership, localization-ready, accessibility | | `design/gdd/**` | Required sections per `modes.workflow`, formula format, edge cases | | `design/narrative/**` | Lore consistency, character voice, canon levels | | `assets/data/**/*.json` | JSON validity, naming conventions, schema rules | | `assets/shaders/**` | Naming conventions, performance targets, cross-platform rules | | `**/*.tscn`, `**/*.tres` | Scene and resource files changed in the editor where possible; safe hand-edit rules | | `tests/**` | Test naming, coverage requirements, fixture patterns | | `prototypes/**` | Relaxed standards, README required, hypothesis documented | ## Design Philosophy This template is grounded in professional game development practices: - **MDA Framework** — Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics analysis for game design - **Self-Determination Theory** — Autonomy, Competence, Relatedness for player motivation - **Flow State Design** — Challenge-skill balance for player engagement - **Bartle Player Types** — Audience targeting and validation - **Verification-Driven Development** — Tests first, then implementation ## Customization This is a **template**, not a locked framework. Everything is meant to be customized: - **Add/remove agents** — delete agent files you don't need, add new ones for your domains - **Edit agent prompts** — tune agent behavior, add project-specific knowledge - **Modify skills** — adjust workflows to match your team's process - **Add rules** — create new path-scoped rules for your project's directory structure - **Tune hooks** — adjust validation strictness, add new checks - **Pick your engine** — use the Godot, Unity, or Unreal agent set (or none) - **Tune process weight** — `modes.rigor` and its underlying knobs in `project.yaml` (see [Configuration](#configuration)). Override per-run with `--review solo` on any skill. ## Platform Support Primary development on **Windows 10** with Git Bash. The hooks and scripts are also tested on **macOS** — its stock bash 3.2 and BSD tools, with and without `jq` — and on **Linux**. All hooks use POSIX-compatible patterns (`grep -E`, not `grep -P`) and include fallbacks for missing tools. The `notify.sh` hook uses PowerShell for Windows toast notifications and is a no-op elsewhere — desktop notifications on macOS/Linux are not yet wired. Please file issues for any platform-specific breakage. ## Community - **Discussions** — [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios/discussions) for questions, ideas, and showcasing what you've built - **Issues** — [Bug reports and feature requests](https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios/issues) --- ## Supporting This Project Claude Code Game Studios is free and open source. If it saves you time or helps you ship your game, consider supporting continued development:

 

- **[Buy Me a Coffee](https://www.buymeacoffee.com/donchitos3)** — one-time support - **[GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/Donchitos)** — recurring support through GitHub Sponsorships help fund time spent maintaining skills, adding new agents, keeping up with Claude Code and engine API changes, and responding to community issues. --- *Built for Claude Code. Maintained and extended — contributions welcome via [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios/discussions).* ## License MIT License. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) for details.

readme:dmux/minilake.text:
MiniLake

Free, open-source local Databricks emulator for offline development and testing.

Real SQL & Spark execution · Unity Catalog hierarchy · Databricks SDK compatible · Terraform compatible · MIT licensed

Website · Documentation · GitHub · Container Image (GHCR)

--- **MiniLake** is a free, local Databricks API emulator — a single-developer tool for testing `databricks-sdk`/Terraform code against real SQL, real Delta Lake, and real Job execution, without paying for cloud compute. ## Quick Start ```bash # Option 1: PyPI pip install minilake minilake --port 8000 # Option 2: GitHub Container Registry docker run -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/dmux/minilake:latest # Option 3: Clone and build git clone https://github.com/dmux/minilake && cd minilake docker compose up -d # Verify (any option) curl http://localhost:8000/_minilake/health ``` Then open **** for the built-in SQL workspace — an Athena-style query editor with a data catalog, saved queries and query history ([details](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/ui.md)). No account, no API key, no sign-up — and the container image downloads nothing at runtime: DuckDB's `delta` extension and the Delta / Unity Catalog Spark jars are baked in at build time, so it works air-gapped ([details](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md#offline-use)). Then point any Databricks client at it: ```python from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient w = WorkspaceClient(host="http://localhost:8000", token="dev") w.catalogs.create(name="vendas") ``` More in [Getting Started](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md). ## Documentation | | | |---|---| | [Getting Started](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md) | Install, first catalog and query, internal endpoints | | [Web UI](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/ui.md) | The built-in SQL workspace at `/ui` | | [Configuration](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/configuration.md) | Every environment variable, persistence, HTTPS/TLS | | [Databricks SDK](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/databricks-sdk.md) | Unity Catalog, warehouses, SQL and jobs from Python | | [Terraform & Asset Bundles](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/terraform.md) | The provider, and `bundle deploy` / `bundle run` | | [Spark & Delta Lake](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/spark-and-delta.md) | Real Delta files, real Spark jobs, `spark.table()` by name | | **[MCP Server](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/mcp/index.md)** | **67 tools for LLM agents — [examples](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/mcp/examples.md), [tool reference](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/mcp/tools.md), [troubleshooting](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/mcp/troubleshooting.md)** | | [Testing & development](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/testing.md) | Running the suite, adding an API group | | [Releases & CI/CD](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/releases.md) | How a tag becomes a published image | | [Feature status](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/FEATURES.md) | Endpoint-by-endpoint status and design rationale | | [API coverage](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/CLI_COVERAGE.md) | Measured: every SDK endpoint probed through the real `databricks` CLI | | [Emulation roadmap](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/EMULATION_ROADMAP.md) | What is worth building next, with measured gap counts | ## Supported Services | Service | Status | Notes | |---|---|---| | **Unity Catalog** (catalogs, schemas, tables, volumes, functions) | ✅ Real | Each catalog = its own DuckDB database (`ATTACH`), native `catalog.schema.table` addressing; a SQL function becomes a real DuckDB macro, callable by its three-part name | | **Unity Catalog metastore** | ✅ Real | One synthetic metastore: `current-metastore-assignment`, `metastore_summary`, list/get | | **EXTERNAL Delta Tables** | ✅ Real | Real Delta files; `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` via a generated Spark job, reads via `delta_scan()` | | **SQL Statement Execution** | ✅ Real | Real DuckDB; `JSON_ARRAY`/`ARROW_STREAM`/`CSV`, `INLINE`/`EXTERNAL_LINKS`; result manifest carries column types | | **SQL Warehouses** | ✅ Real | Full CRUD + lifecycle | | **Query History** | ✅ Real | `w.query_history.list()` over everything executed, failures included | | **Saved Queries** | ✅ Real | `w.queries.*` CRUD with `update_mask` | | **Alerts** | ✅ Real | `w.alerts.*` CRUD; conditions are really evaluated against query results, and back `sql_task.alert` | | **Web UI** | ✅ Real | Athena-style SQL workspace at `/ui` — see [Web UI](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/ui.md) | | **Jobs** | ✅ Real | Sibling Docker container execution (Spark) or subprocess fallback; real DAG scheduling (`depends_on`/`run_if`); `runs/submit` one-shot runs; `sql_task.file`/`.query`/`.alert` all execute for real | | **Workspace** | ✅ Real | File-backed notebook/script storage; raw-bytes `workspace-files` sync powers `databricks bundle deploy` / `bundle run` | | **DBFS & Files API** | ✅ Real | File-backed storage, chunked upload | | **Secrets** | ✅ Real | Real CRUD; values only resolvable inside job env vars, never via direct API (matches real Databricks). Scope ACLs are stored and read back, never enforced | | **Clusters** | ✅ Real state machine | CRUD + timed lifecycle transitions, `update`/`pin`/`unpin`; **no real Spark compute** (by design) | | **Cluster policies & instance pools** | ✅ Real CRUD | Resolve and validate against clusters; never enforced — there is no compute to constrain | | **Permissions** | ✅ Real CRUD | Single-user "allow-all" default (by design — see Gaps) | | **UC Grants** | ✅ Real CRUD | `w.grants.*` and `databricks_grants`, with real privilege **inheritance** (a catalog grant is effective on its schemas and tables); never enforced | | **Workspace admin** | ✅ Real CRUD | Git credentials, IP access lists, global init scripts, notification destinations, instance profiles, `workspace-conf` — stored and read back, never enforced | | **Legacy SQL (`preview/sql`)** | ✅ Real | Queries, alerts, dashboards, widgets, visualizations, data sources — adapters over the modern stores, so both surfaces see one object | | **Identity & SCIM** | ✅ Real CRUD | Current user, plus Users/Groups/ServicePrincipals CRUD, SCIM `PATCH` and filtering. Identities are records, not credentials — see Gaps | | **Tokens** | ✅ Real | `w.tokens.*`; the value is returned once, as in the real API — but authenticates nothing | | **Persistence** (`MINILAKE_PERSIST=1`) | ✅ Real | JSON snapshot on shutdown, restored on startup | | **Unity Catalog protocol for Spark** | ✅ Real | `spark.table("cat.sch.tbl")` resolves against minilake — see [Spark & Delta Lake](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/spark-and-delta.md#reading-by-name-with-unity-catalog) | | **JupyterLab + PySpark + Delta** (optional) | ✅ Real | `docker compose --profile notebook up` | | **MCP Server** (optional, `MINILAKE_MCP=1`) | ✅ Real | 67 tools + resources + prompts at `/mcp` — see [MCP Server](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/mcp/index.md) | | Repos, multi-language notebooks, DBT/pipeline tasks, DLT, Model Registry, Vector Search, Lakeview/Genie, Delta Sharing | 🚫 Not implemented | Returns `501 NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. For the measured picture, see [API coverage](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/docs/CLI_COVERAGE.md) | ## Known Gaps These are **deliberate**, not oversights — minilake targets one developer running it locally, not a shared or multi-tenant server: - **No real authentication** — any token is accepted. SCIM identities and personal access tokens are records, not credentials: creating a user makes no way to sign in, and revoking a token locks nobody out. - **No access-control enforcement** — the Permissions API is real CRUD but always allow-all, so a test that passes here says nothing about grants in a real workspace. - **No real Spark compute for Clusters** — state machine only; real compute happens through Jobs' sibling containers instead. - **Single process, no HA** — and DuckDB's single-writer model means concurrent load contends on locks. - **Uneven test coverage** — `jobs.py`, `sql_statements.py` and `unity_catalog.py` are covered mostly on happy paths, not edge cases. ## Contributing See [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for the project structure, how to add a new API group, and the PR checklist. ## License MIT — see [LICENSE](https://github.com/dmux/minilake/blob/main/LICENSE).

readme:yc-software/minecraft-agent-harne.text:
minecraft-agent-harness

LLM agents that play Minecraft.

Quickstart · Configuration · Tools · Teams · Bed Wars example

Point an LLM at a Minecraft server and give it something to do. It plays through [Mineflayer](https://github.com/PrismarineJS/mineflayer), so it walks, mines, crafts, builds, fights and chats like a regular player. [pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi) handles the model session. We've run Bed Wars matches with it, and a survival server with 50 agents on it at once. What's in here: - Claude, GPT, Gemini, OpenRouter, or your own endpoint if it speaks the OpenAI Responses API - Sessions that survive restarts. Kill an agent, start it again under the same name, and it carries on - A shell for every agent (Docker, E2B or a plain local folder). Agents keep notes there and write little scripts that call their own game tools - Teams from a single JSON file, with DMs between agents and an optional shared machine - Vision, if you want it (experimental) ## Quickstart You'll need Node 22.19+, an API key for some model provider, and a Minecraft server. If you don't have a server, the repo comes with a dev one, which needs Java 21. ```sh npm ci cp .env.example .env # add the API key for your model provider npm run server # Paper 1.21.6 on localhost:25565, offline mode ``` Then in a second terminal: ```sh npm start -- --objective "Gather wood and build a small shelter near spawn" ``` That's it. The default model is GPT-6.1 Terra, and [Configuration](docs/configuration.md#model) covers the other providers and how to switch. Join `localhost:25565` from Minecraft 1.21.6 if you want to watch, and `/tell Agent ` to talk to it. Its output and tool calls stream to the terminal. `Ctrl+C` stops it. Everything it knows lives in `.agent-state//`, so starting it again with the same name resumes the session. ### Your own server ```sh npm start -- --host play.example.net --port 25565 --objective "Mine iron" ``` Online-mode servers need `--auth microsoft` (you'll get a sign-in prompt). Agents assume survival; pass `--game-mode` if your server puts them in something else. ### Docker Fill in `.env` as above, then: ```sh docker compose up ``` You get a Paper server on `localhost:25565` and one agent. Change what it does with `AGENT_OBJECTIVE` in `.env`. State goes in the `agent-state` volume. Already have a server? Just run the agent image: ```sh docker build -t minecraft-agent . docker run --rm -it --env-file .env -v agent-state:/data minecraft-agent --host play.example.net -o "Mine iron" ``` ### Teams ```sh npm start -- team examples/team.json ``` Starts three agents who can message each other. [Team config](docs/multi-agent.md) has the details. For something with rules and a referee, look at the [Bed Wars example](examples/bedwars/README.md). ## Configuration Flags, environment variables (`.env` works) or a JSON file via `--config`. Flags win over env vars, env vars win over the file. A heads-up about the shell: agents get one by default. That's E2B if `E2B_API_KEY` is set, otherwise Docker if it's running, otherwise a local folder, and local means commands run as you. Use `--sandbox none` if you'd rather they didn't have one. More docs: - [Configuration](docs/configuration.md): models, auth, sandboxes, vision, where files go - [Tools](docs/tools.md): everything an agent can do - [Architecture](docs/architecture.md): how the code fits together ## Development ```sh npm run check # lint, format, tests ``` [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) covers the rest. ## License MIT. Some of the skill library comes from [Mindcraft](https://github.com/kolbytn/mindcraft) and the renderer worker from [prismarine-viewer](https://github.com/PrismarineJS/prismarine-viewer); their licenses are in [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

page:https://labs.ycombinator.com/projec.text:
Agents in Games · Labs 
     
     
   
 
 
 
 
 
 
     
   
   
     
       
         
       
       
         Home 
         Projects 
         QM 
         Contact 
       
     

     
          Agents in Games    Minecraft    Civ50    Bed Wars      Mindustry    The setup    What we saw    Funny bloopers    Run your own swarm    Open questions      
       
         
           Agents in Games 
           October 2026 
         

          Note:  We're running a new Minecraft colony with 25 GPT-6.1 Terra agents.  Follow on Twitch  

         Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice). 

         We teamed up with  Olam Labs , which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry. 

         Minecraft 

         Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's  video pretraining work  to Google DeepMind's agents  defeating the Ender Dragon . 

         We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game. 

          github.com/yc-software/minecraft-agent-harness  

           Civ50 

         50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs. 

         The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages. 

         At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access. 

            plans/settlement.md  Download    Settlement coordination (Ada)
Primary storage Greta: (1526,70,1507), crafting table (1526,70,1505).
Other storage Mabel: double chest (1510,71,1516); Cleo: (1526,71,1523).
Cleo building hub shelter; Bram stone mining.
Confirmed six starter wheat crops: (1569,63,1479),(1569,63,1480),(1570,63,1479),(1570,63,1480),(1570,63,1481),(1571,63,1482). Preserve farmland, expand riverside farming. Do not harvest immature wheat.
Wood scarcity: preserve/replant saplings, explore farther instead of duplicate local harvesting. Nursery around spawn and south-west.
Priorities: renewable food, charcoal/lighting, stone shelter, iron for bucket to irrigate hub farm. Avoid redundant new storage.
Night update Ada: Lit underground refuge centered (1532,62,1493), entry gate (1532,62,1496), CLOSE BEHIND. Cobble flanks secured x1531/1533 y62–63 z1496. Surface staircase starts (1532,69,1500); Cleo repairing. Food kitchen furnace (1527,62,1493); table (1528,62,1493). Tamsin coordinates food priorities and dawn hunting (Hugo+Rafe). Basil health9.5 food6 urgent; Esme health8 food16; Tamsin health9 food15. Silas holds hoe, Zane plants riverside at dawn. Logs: Tove delivered29 oak to chest (1511,71,1516). Forest east (1700,68,1508), NW grove (1380–1420,z1380). Preserve saplings and livestock breeding pairs. Avoid night surface: witch near (1527,71,1512).
    Ada’s settlement plan, from the archived shared machine.  
        Following Vera during the first night, 8:09–12:05 into the run, at 2x speed.

           Bed Wars 

         We ran nine 45-minute games of Bed Wars. The teams were 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents with the instruction: "win the game." GPTs won our series 6–3, usually by breaking Claude's bed in the final minutes, while Claude played defensively and tried to win on kills. 

         Bed Wars is a popular game format where teams fight to destroy each other’s bed while protecting their own. In our instance, teams started on separate islands, with currency spawners between them in no-man’s-land. Agents could build bridges to cross between islands and buy upgrades using currency collected in the center of the map. 

         A team wins by destroying the opposing side’s bed, then killing their remaining players. As long as a team’s bed is present, players respawn after dying. Once a team’s bed is destroyed, their players no longer respawn, meaning their next death eliminates them from the match. This may seem complicated, but think of the team’s main objective as defending their bed and destroying their opponent’s. That said, if no beds were destroyed in a given match, the team with the most kills won. 

         In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed. This was an inherently riskier strategy vs. Claude’s more defensive posture that tried to win by kill count. 

         Takeaways 

         The two teams had very different communication styles. GPT almost immediately started using truncated forms of speech: “First leg complete x32 z9..24 y100.” Claude signed its name and said "we" (30% of messages, against GPT's 5%). GPT sent 5-30x more messages. Its most-messaged player got 198–368 DMs a game; Claude's got 11–48.

         GPT agents came up with much more aggressive and elaborate strategies. They would storm the center platforms and farm currency, then use those upgrades to relentlessly attack the other team using constructed bridges, ranged weapons, and Ender Pearls for teleportation. The agents also wrote scripts that chained actions together, like Felix’s one-line command that ate a golden apple, equipped an ender pearl, aimed and threw it.
