         Mindustry 

  Game replay:  
 
  Click “AI-generated transcript analysis” to view an analysis of the team discussions, strategies, etc. for each game!  
  Use the panel on the right (tabs “Claude chat”, “GPT chat” and “Agents”) to watch a team or a specific agent’s live chat and transcripts in sync with the timeline.  
  Use the + and - buttons on the map to zoom in and watch them up close.  
 
        Fullscreen     ×  
 The GPTs (GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex) won 6-1 against the Claudes (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code) in the 7 games. The series ran for about 9.5 hours, with game 3 being the most intense and closest at 4 hours 16 minutes. Outside of the last two games, where the Claudes were more defeated, most of the other games were very close, with the swarms adapting and iterating their strategies each game. 
 The setup 
  Mindustry  is an open source game by Anuken. Full credit to him for the amazing game and letting it be open source for cool experiments like this! 
 It’s a factory-building game with tower defense and real-time strategy: you mine resources, build conveyor supply chains and factories, and turn that economy into turrets and an army. In its PvP mode, which we used, two teams race to build the stronger economy and military and destroy the other team’s core. 
 This makes it a great environment for testing multi-agent dynamics. Mindustry is 2D, so it can be played easily by agents, is replayable, and is prone to adversarial pressures that can test these swarms under competitive social conditions that they may face in the real world. 
 We structured the simulated environment to have two teams of agents spawn on each side of a map, with the same resources on both sides. They play a best of N series, where you set how many games the teams play. When launching it, we set the composition of the teams (which harness + model, and how many), then let it run! The agents run in their own sandbox and the game is exposed to them through an API, so they are able to run scripts and interact with the game however they like in their own Linux environment. 
 Both teams have the exact same API to the game, without any special instructions given to them on how to play - neither team is given anything more than the other team. 
 
Multi-agent swarms, like in  the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident , can turn simple adversarial conditions, like being in a sandbox with an unsolvable task, into a hive-minded ecology of agents that take over compute clusters, hack Hugging Face, and more. Studying how these swarms operate in reproducible game environments like Mindustry that mimic real-world scenarios can be both crucial (and fascinating) to understanding what these systems may look like in our future. 
 What we saw 
 #1 GPTs act more like a hive 
 GPTs appeared to be much more collaborative and willing to do grunt work. They were more willing to dedicate themselves towards the collective “goal” (winning). 
 #2 Claudes had one leader, GPTs divided ownership with small slices 
 Because GPT models seemed to be more hive-mind-like, they formed much stronger communication networks within the swarm. They communicated with more agents on average, much more frequently. Though a lot of the communication for GPTs was low value (alerts, info, what they did, etc.), Claudes were much more effective with their communication, using it in a way more similar to how humans might communicate in Slack. 
   Each dot is an agent, sized by the messages it sent; lines show each agent’s strongest ties. Leaders are named.  
 #3 GPTs spoke with increasingly compressed phrases without spaces, Claudes voted with +1 in a more democratic-like decision process 
 The language of GPTs within swarms seemed to get compressed and more specialized as time went on, forming their own nicknames for events and things that the entire hive abided by. 
              Game 7, at about 38:40: the Claude team chat (top) and the GPT team chat (bottom), scrolling in the replay. GPT messages like “G7T5FIRSTcourierLIVE” run words together.  
 The Claudes adopted a much more democratic “+1” system, where, in order to propose their next major plans, they would put up proposals and others would put “+1” if they agreed. If they did not agree, they would have a (brief) debate on why it’s a bad idea, and the proposal would end there. Proposals that went through typically got many “+1”s without pushback. 
   Left, spaces as a share of each team’s chat characters in each game; right, the 28 Claudes who answered one focus-fire proposal with +1 in game 6, plotted by minute.  
 #4 Roles harden, leaders stay put 
 As games went on and the teams adapted, they specialized into their roles further. Leaders typically stayed, and major shifts in roles only happened when losing. The Claudes never switched leaders or hierarchy despite losing many games in a row. When games got close, GPT models always had some agents taking initiative with their own attack or taking command of some part of the army in order to not lose - a similar behavior was not observed among the Claudes. 
   Filled dots mark who led the army or fleet in each game, hollow dots who proposed rules, and the dot under each game is its winner, grey for Claude and off-white for GPT.  
 #5 When stuck, GPTs read the source code 
 When games got intense and it was ambiguous, GPT agents would fetch the public code of Mindustry from the web (which was allowed in their sandbox) and try to write scripts, analyze for weaknesses, etc. This did not let them alter the source code of the game; it was just a way for them to understand all the units and mechanics at a source level. The GPTs openly collaborated in their chat, discussing what unit or code they found that they could potentially use to switch up strategies. This was never disallowed, but they were never told to do this either. The Claudes never searched up game code from the web. 
   Source files fetched and chat messages citing the source per 10 minutes of game time, with games drawn to scale.  
 Funny Bloopers 
 
  Game 1, minute 5: Claude #1 tested hand-mining coal and posted “…RETRACT my coal proposal…”. Four seconds later Claude #37 answered with a measurement (“…core coal went 124 -> 1235 in 35s.…”), and Claude #1 conceded: “…My bad twice - seat-37 is right, hand-mining coal works…”  
  Game 3: the GPTs apologize in their compressed shorthand too. After wrongly claiming a Corvus couldn’t hit air, GPT #80 posted “80 CORRECTION: myCorvusCANNOT-AIR assertion wasWRONG…” and signed off with “…Sorryforbad tacticalclaim.” After a mix-up over who was flying a Corvus, GPT #87 wrote “…Sorryforthisavoidableconflict; noadvanceordersfrom87again.”  
  Game 5: at the very second the Claude core died, GPT #62 posted “62 G5 first-wave loss observed…”. A teammate corrected it 28 seconds into game 6: it was a win.  
  After losing game 6 to the zenith strike, Claude #22 found that 55 of the team’s 74 anti-air duo turrets had been loaded with copper instead of graphite: “…55 of them were loaded with COPPER…”. In game 7 the Claudes built a ring of 207 duos fed with graphite, and it stopped the same 24-zenith strike.  
  Game 7: the GPTs closed the series to nine decimal places: “100 OFFICIALSERIESFINAL: G7 WIN3413.394082916s, Crux6000/6000 vsSharded0.…” (Crux is GPT’s team, Sharded is Claude’s).  
 
              The same 24-zenith strike on the Claude core, in game 6, where it gets through, and in game 7, after the Claudes switched their anti-air duos from copper to graphite.  
 How to run your own swarm (we open sourced it!) 
 
  Multi-Agent Mindustry : the game environments from this post. To get started, read the README, or give the link to your agent with “help me understand and set this up”, as we’ve included everything it needs. It requires just a model provider API + a harness + compute (e.g. locally on your MacBook or remote sandboxes) to run. 
  Multi-Agent Harbor : the framework that runs them, our fork of  Harbor , the open-source framework behind Terminal-Bench. Our fork runs multiple agents in any environment. We use it for a variety of things (enterprises, industrials, etc.), and it’s very useful for game-based multi-agent simulations like this one. For more on the framework, point your agent at it. 
 
 Multi-Agent Mindustry comes with two environments. One is a best of N series like this run, with teams composed however you like from generic coding-agent harnesses and models, for example 5 Claudes + 5 GPTs against 5 Geminis + 5 Groks in a best of 5. The other, Endless Survival, has one team of up to 20 agents hold off endless enemy waves. 
 We intentionally do no harness-level customization or special memory work. Each agent gets its own Linux environment, a generic harness and the game’s API, writes scripts and takes notes as it pleases, and relies on the harness’s native compaction (which is quite good). Nobody tells it how to play, so it’s free to specialize, play and (optionally) try whatever it wants. This tests models the way they’re used in the real world, in a setup similar to swarm-like situations like the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, and it’s reproducible and legible, since most people know the popular harnesses and can replicate work like this themselves. 
 Open Questions 
 
  Combining model families  
  How hierarchies change based on the model composition of a team  
  Can a large swarm of less capable agents beat a swarm of more capable ones? (how swarm size and capability trade off)  
  Which models get the most powerful as the swarm grows?  
  How different initial prompts affect the swarm  
  Different communication setups: what if they could talk to the enemy team? What if they couldn’t talk to their own team?  
 
       
     

     
       Building something?  Apply to YC .

cna:CVE-2026-109516.desc: The Bot for Telegram on WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass leading to Account Takeover in all versions up to, and including, 1.3.0. The `/wp-json/woo-telegram/v1/main/` REST endpoint is registered with `permission_callback => '__return_true'` and performs no Telegram webhook signature verification, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to POST a forged bot update with a `message.chat.id` set to any WordPress login name; `bftow_get_user_system_id()` resolves this attacker-supplied value to the targeted account via `get_user_by('login', $tgId)` with no ownership proof, and writes a login token computed as `md5($_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT'] . time())` — both inputs are fully attacker-controlled or bounded within seconds using the response's own `Date` header. The resulting token is redeemable at the unauthenticated, capability-check-free, and nonce-less `?action=bftow_create_order&bftow_token=` endpoint, which calls `wp_set_auth_cookie()` unconditionally via `login_user_by_id`, issuing a persistent authenticated session cookie for the targeted account to the attacker. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to log in as any WordPress user, including administrators, given only that user's username.

# Skills For Real Engineers [![skills.sh](https://skills.sh/b/mattpocock/skills)](https://skills.sh/mattpocock/skills) My agent skills that I use every day to do real engineering - not vibe coding. Developing real applications is hard. Approaches like GSD, BMAD, and Spec-Kit try to help by owning the process. But while doing so, they take away your control and make bugs in the process hard to resolve. These skills are designed to be small, easy to adapt, and composable. They work with any model. They're based on decades of engineering experience. Hack around with them. Make them your own. Enjoy. If you want to keep up with changes to these skills, and any new ones I create, you can join ~60,000 other devs on my newsletter: [Sign Up To The Newsletter](https://www.aihero.dev/s/skills-newsletter) ## Installation (30-second setup) A plugin updates itself. [skills.sh](https://skills.sh/mattpocock/skills) copies editable files into your project, and you update them by hand. Pick one per agent, because installing both gives you every skill twice. ### 1. Get the skills
Claude Code ```bash claude plugin install mattpocock-skills@claude-plugins-official ``` Updates itself by default.
Codex ```bash codex plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills codex plugin add mattpocock-skills@mattpocock ``` Updates itself at startup.
GitHub Copilot (CLI and VS Code) ```bash copilot plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills copilot plugin install mattpocock-skills@mattpocock ``` Then, once, add to `~/.copilot/settings.json`: ```json { "extraKnownMarketplaces": { "mattpocock": { "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "mattpocock/skills" }, "autoUpdate": true } } } ``` In VS Code, run **Chat: Install Plugin From Source** and enter `https://github.com/mattpocock/skills`. It updates daily.
Gemini CLI (manual updates) ```bash gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/engineering gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/productivity ``` Re-run both commands to update.
Any other agent, or editable files (manual updates) ```bash npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills -a # cursor, opencode, devin, windsurf, amp, pi; omit -a to choose ``` When the installer asks which skills to take, include `setup-matt-pocock-skills`. To update, run `npx skills@latest update`, and re-run `add` to pick up new skills.
### 2. Run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` In your agent, run it once per repo. It will: - Ask you which issue tracker you want to use (GitHub, GitLab, local files, or anything else you describe) - Ask you what labels you apply to tickets when you triage them (`/triage` uses labels) - Ask you where you want to save any docs we create ### 3. Bam - you're ready to go. ## Why These Skills Exist I built these skills as a way to fix common failure modes I see with Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents. ### #1: The Agent Didn't Do What I Want > "No-one knows exactly what they want" > > David Thomas & Andrew Hunt, [The Pragmatic Programmer](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Pragmatic-Programmer-Anniversary-Journey-Mastery/dp/B0833F1T3V) **The Problem**. The most common failure mode in software development is misalignment. You think the dev knows what you want. Then you see what they've built - and you realize it didn't understand you at all. This is just the same in the AI age. There is a communication gap between you and the agent. The fix for this is a **grilling session** - getting the agent to ask you detailed questions about what you're building. **The Fix** is to use: - [`/grill-me`](./skills/productivity/grill-me/SKILL.md) - for non-code uses - [`/grill-with-docs`](./skills/engineering/grill-with-docs/SKILL.md) - same as [`/grill-me`](./skills/productivity/grill-me/SKILL.md), but adds more goodies (see below) These are my most popular skills. They help you align with the agent before you get started, and think deeply about the change you're making. Use them _every_ time you want to make a change. ### #2: The Agent Is Way Too Verbose > With a ubiquitous language, conversations among developers and expressions of the code are all derived from the same domain model. > > Eric Evans, [Domain-Driven-Design](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Domain-Driven-Design-Tackling-Complexity-Software/dp/0321125215) **The Problem**: At the start of a project, devs and the people they're building the software for (the domain experts) are usually speaking different languages. I felt the same tension with my agents. Agents are usually dropped into a project and asked to figure out the jargon as they go. So they use 20 words where 1 will do. **The Fix** for this is a shared language. It's a document that helps agents decode the jargon used in the project.
Example Here's an example [glossary](https://github.com/mattpocock/course-video-manager/blob/076a5a7a182db0fe1e62971dd7a68bcadf010f1c/CONTEXT.md) (still named `CONTEXT.md` at that pinned commit, from before the skills renamed the convention), from my `course-video-manager` repo. Which one is easier to read? - **BEFORE**: "There's a problem when a lesson inside a section of a course is made 'real' (i.e. given a spot in the file system)" - **AFTER**: "There's a problem with the materialization cascade" This concision pays off session after session.
This is built into [`/grill-with-docs`](./skills/engineering/grill-with-docs/SKILL.md). It's a grilling session, but that helps you build a shared language with the AI, and document hard-to-explain decisions in ADR's. It's hard to explain how powerful this is. It might be the single coolest technique in this repo. Try it, and see. > [!TIP] > A shared language has many other benefits than reducing verbosity: > > - **Variables, functions and files are named consistently**, using the shared language > - As a result, the **codebase is easier to navigate** for the agent > - The agent also **spends fewer tokens on thinking**, because it has access to a more concise language ### #3: The Code Doesn't Work > "Always take small, deliberate steps. The rate of feedback is your speed limit. Never take on a task that’s too big." > > David Thomas & Andrew Hunt, [The Pragmatic Programmer](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Pragmatic-Programmer-Anniversary-Journey-Mastery/dp/B0833F1T3V) **The Problem**: Let's say that you and the agent are aligned on what to build. What happens when the agent _still_ produces crap? It's time to look at your feedback loops. Without feedback on how the code it produces actually runs, the agent will be flying blind. **The Fix**: You need the usual tranche of feedback loops: static types, browser access, and automated tests. For automated tests, a red-green-refactor loop is critical. This is where the agent writes a failing test first, then fixes the test. This helps give the agent a consistent level of feedback that results in far better code. I've built a **[`/tdd`](./skills/engineering/tdd/SKILL.md) skill** you can slot into any project. It encourages red-green-refactor and gives the agent plenty of guidance on what makes good and bad tests. For debugging, I've also built a **[`/diagnosing-bugs`](./skills/engineering/diagnosing-bugs/SKILL.md)** skill that wraps best debugging practices into a disciplined loop, gated phase by phase. ### #4: We Built A Ball Of Mud > "Invest in the design of the system _every day_." > > Kent Beck, [Extreme Programming Explained](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Extreme-Programming-Explained-Embrace-Change/dp/0321278658) > "The best modules are deep. They allow a lot of functionality to be accessed through a simple interface." > > John Ousterhout, [A Philosophy Of Software Design](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Philosophy-Software-Design-2nd/dp/173210221X) **The Problem**: Most apps built with agents are complex and hard to change. Because agents can radically speed up coding, they also accelerate software entropy. Codebases get more complex at an unprecedented rate. **The Fix** for this is a radical new approach to AI-powered development: caring about the design of the code. This is built in to every layer of these skills: - [`/to-spec`](./skills/engineering/to-spec/SKILL.md) quizzes you about which modules you're touching before creating a spec And crucially, [`/improve-codebase-architecture`](./skills/engineering/improve-codebase-architecture/SKILL.md) surveys a codebase for deepening opportunities and hands you the candidates. I recommend running it on your codebase once every few days. It is a survey, not a rescue: on a genuinely old codebase it will find real candidates, but it won't untangle the mud for you. ### Summary Software engineering fundamentals matter more than ever. These skills are my best effort at condensing these fundamentals into repeatable practices, to help you ship the best apps of your career. Enjoy. ## Reference These split on one axis: who can invoke them. **User-invoked** skills are reachable only when you type them (e.g. `/grill-me`); their job is to orchestrate. **Model-invoked** skills can be invoked by you _or_ reached for automatically by the agent when the task fits; they hold the reusable discipline. A user-invoked skill may invoke model-invoked skills, but never another user-invoked one. ### Engineering Skills I use daily for code work. **User-invoked** - **[ask-matt](./skills/engineering/ask-matt/SKILL.md)**: Ask which skill or flow fits your situation. A router over the user-invoked skills in this repo. - **[grill-with-docs](./skills/engineering/grill-with-docs/SKILL.md)**: Grilling session that also builds your project's domain model, sharpening terminology and updating `GLOSSARY.md` and ADRs inline. - **[triage](./skills/engineering/triage/SKILL.md)**: Move issues through a state machine of triage roles. - **[improve-codebase-architecture](./skills/engineering/improve-codebase-architecture/SKILL.md)**: Scan a codebase for deepening opportunities, present them as a visual HTML report, then grill through whichever one you pick. - **[setup-matt-pocock-skills](./skills/engineering/setup-matt-pocock-skills/SKILL.md)**: Configure this repo for the engineering skills (issue tracker, triage labels, domain doc layout). Run once per repo before using the other engineering skills. - **[to-spec](./skills/engineering/to-spec/SKILL.md)**: Turn the current conversation into a spec and publish it to the issue tracker. No interview, just synthesizes what you've already discussed. - **[to-tickets](./skills/engineering/to-tickets/SKILL.md)**: Break any plan, spec, or conversation into a set of tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its blocking edges, written as text in a local file, or as native blocking links on a real tracker. - **[implement](./skills/engineering/implement/SKILL.md)**: Build the work described by a spec or set of tickets, driving `/tdd` at pre-agreed seams and closing out with `/code-review` before committing. - **[implement-spec](./skills/engineering/implement-spec/SKILL.md)**: Implement a whole spec on one integration branch. Works the tickets as a task graph, running implementer subagents across the ready frontier for maximum concurrency, then closes out with `/code-review`. - **[wayfinder](./skills/engineering/wayfinder/SKILL.md)**: Plan a huge chunk of work, more than one agent session can hold, as a shared map of decision tickets on the issue tracker, and resolve them one at a time until the way to the destination is clear. - **[retro](./skills/engineering/retro/SKILL.md)**: Suggest improvements to the coding agent's environment (navigation, automated checks, coding standards, steering files, tooling) after a session, most severe first. **Model-invoked** - **[prototype](./skills/engineering/prototype/SKILL.md)**: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question, either a single shareable HTML file for state/logic questions, or several radically different UI variations toggleable from one route. - **[diagnosing-bugs](./skills/engineering/diagnosing-bugs/SKILL.md)**: Disciplined diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions: build a feedback loop that goes red on this bug → minimise → hypothesise → instrument → fix → regression-test. - **[research](./skills/engineering/research/SKILL.md)**: Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a cited Markdown file in the repo, run as a background agent. - **[tdd](./skills/engineering/tdd/SKILL.md)**: Test-driven development with a red-green-refactor loop. Builds features or fixes bugs one vertical slice at a time. - **[domain-modeling](./skills/engineering/domain-modeling/SKILL.md)**: Actively build and sharpen a project's domain model: challenge terms against the glossary, stress-test with edge-case scenarios, and update `GLOSSARY.md` and ADRs inline. - **[codebase-design](./skills/engineering/codebase-design/SKILL.md)**: Shared discipline and vocabulary for designing deep modules: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface. - **[code-review](./skills/engineering/code-review/SKILL.md)**: Two-axis review of the diff since a fixed point: **Standards** (does it follow the repo's coding standards, plus a Fowler smell baseline?) and **Spec** (does it faithfully implement the originating issue/spec?), run as parallel sub-agents so neither pollutes the other. - **[pr](./skills/engineering/pr/SKILL.md)**: The shape a pull request body should take: a summary as the smallest visual that makes the change clear, before/after evidence that it works, and a merge-danger call (one-way or two-way door, plus blast radius). - **[wizard](./skills/engineering/wizard/SKILL.md)**: Generate an interactive bash wizard that walks a human through steps only they can perform: provisioning infrastructure, setting up credentials or CI secrets, walking an unfamiliar third-party dashboard, or running a one-off migration or cutover. ### Productivity General workflow tools, not code-specific. **User-invoked** - **[grill-me](./skills/productivity/grill-me/SKILL.md)**: Get relentlessly interviewed about a plan or design until every branch of the design tree is resolved. - **[handoff](./skills/productivity/handoff/SKILL.md)**: Compact the current conversation into a handoff document so another agent can continue the work. - **[teach](./skills/productivity/teach/SKILL.md)**: Teach the user a new skill or concept over multiple sessions, using the current directory as a stateful teaching workspace. - **[to-questionnaire](./skills/productivity/to-questionnaire/SKILL.md)**: Turn a decision you can't answer alone into a Markdown questionnaire for the one person who can, filled in async, or together over a meeting. It grills you about the send (who it's for, what you need back), not the subject. - **[wait-what](./skills/productivity/wait-what/SKILL.md)**: Fire this the moment a message doesn't land. The agent re-pitches it with the context you're missing, in plain English, using your `GLOSSARY.md` vocabulary. **Model-invoked** - **[grilling](./skills/productivity/grilling/SKILL.md)**: Interview the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea until every branch of the design tree is resolved. The reusable interview primitive behind `grill-me`, `grill-with-docs`, `triage`, `wayfinder` and `improve-codebase-architecture`. - **[writing-for-agents](./skills/productivity/writing-for-agents/SKILL.md)**: Writing documents for agents: skills, AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, and any doc an agent reaches by a pointer.

											 Alert 
										 
 CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog 
 
																																				   




 
   Release Date   October 30, 2026   

  
 
																								 
				  
			 
					 
	 
 
     
     
                      

 
       
  
  
   
           CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its  Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. 
 
  CVE-2026-111357  Ivanti Connect Secure Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability 
  CVE-2026-118527  Ivanti Connect Secure Generation of Predictable Numbers or Identifiers Vulnerability 
 
 These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.  
  Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk  establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.  
 While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of  KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the  specified criteria .  
 Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s  KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

									 Threat Intelligence 
								 
							
															 
									A Series of Unauthenticated Events: Chained Exploitation of Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Days								 

								 October 13, 2026 

																	 Charlie Gardner, Sean Koessel, Steven Adair, and Volexity Volcano Team 
																					 
					 

									 
			 
		 
	 
 
	 
	 

	
	 
		 
			 
				
				
									 
						  [Update:   At the time of publication, Ivanti was in the process of developing a patch for the privilege escalation vulnerability described in this blog post  . On October 29, 2026, Ivanti published a patch that addresses this vulnerability, which is tracked as CVE-2026-111357. Further details are available in  Ivanti’s advisory . The remaining text of this blog post has not been updated.]  
 
   Volexity has identified active in-the-wild exploitation of a vulnerability chain allowing unauthenticated remote code execution in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN devices. Ivanti has  published an advisory  providing upgrade instructions to customers. Systems exhibiting signs of compromise, such as attempts to move laterally originating from the ICS VPN device, should be forensically investigated to ensure no breach has occurred.   
 
 In the first week of October 2026, Volexity discovered an unknown threat actor, UTA0576, abusing a zero-day exploit chain to compromise a fully patched (at the time, version 22.8R2.4) Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) VPN appliance. This exploit chain combined an authentication bypass, a remote code execution (RCE), and a privilege escalation vulnerability to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution. The RCE and authentication bypass vulnerabilities are tracked under CVE-2026-104935. 
 Volexity identified a range of post-exploitation actions undertaken by the threat actor that targeted Active Directory credentials and secrets, including Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) passwords and BitLocker recovery keys. Volexity began working closely with Ivanti as soon as it suspected a vulnerability chain. 
 Since UTA0576 deleted evidence of exploitation from Ivanti debug logs and Linux audit logs, forensic analysis was necessary to discover how the ICS VPN appliance had been compromised. Volexity worked with Ivanti to collect memory and disk images of the impacted device along with analyzing core dumps that were generated as a result of exploitation. Volexity leveraged the core dumps and system memory collections with  Volexity Volcano  to identify and reconstruct the full exploit chain used by the threat actor. UTA0576 also passed commands and results through the exploit chain’s HTTPS requests rather than a separate command-and-control (C2) channel, with no backdoor or web shell deployed to the compromised device. 
 Analysis 
 On October 5, 2026, Volexity began an investigation into suspected malicious activity at a Network Security Monitoring customer. Initial work identified an ICS VPN appliance as the root cause, and subsequent checks confirmed that the ICS VPN appliance was fully patched (22.8R2.4, Build 19097). 
 Volexity conducted a thorough forensic investigation and identified a zero-day exploit chain targeting the following vulnerabilities: 
 
 An authentication bypass in ICS  welcome.cgi  allowing requests to be routed to arbitrary CGI files, including those protected by authentication 
 A file write vulnerability in  wu.cgi  
 A privilege escalation vulnerability in how the ICS  dsinvoked  broker trusts  DSCache  configuration data, which enables an attacker to execute commands as root 
 
 Volexity discovered that starting on October 3, 2026, UTA0576 repeatedly exploited these vulnerabilities to compromise the ICS VPN appliance and run commands on it. With this access, the threat actor undertook the following post-exploitation actions: 
 
 Extracted credentials stored on the ICS VPN appliance, such as domain credentials used with LDAP 
 Dumped and exfiltrated limited Active Directory metadata 
 Deployed a custom Kerberos tool capable of  Kerberoast  attacks and credential testing 
 Deployed a custom Python LDAP tool to search Active Directory for LAPS local administrator passwords, BitLocker recovery keys, and password-bearing attributes via a compromised Active Directory service account 
 Local DNS and host reconnaissance 
 Collected ICS VPN appliance configuration data, including authentication methods 
  Password spraying  
 Packet capture of LDAP traffic from the compromised ICS VPN appliance 
 Inspection of authentication logs to identify valid usernames 
 
 Authentication Bypass 
 The first exploit abused by UTA0576 targets a vulnerability in how the ICS VPN appliance routes requests from front- and back-end processes to a CGI script handler. The following is a high-level overview of how this works: 
 
 The attacker sends a network request to  /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi .
 
 This script is public and serves a login page for the ICS VPN appliance. These requests are therefore allowed without authentication. 
 
 
 This network request names a different script in its headers,  X-DSCGI-PATH: /home/webserver/htdocs/dana/fb/smb/wu.cgi .
 
 This script is not public and executes within a trusted context on the ICS VPN appliance. 
 
 
 The URL is used to determine whether the request is allowed, while the header path is used to determine the destination of the request. From this, the attacker is able to pass requests to the  cgi  script. 
 
 Remote Code Execution 
  The RCE portion of the exploitation chain lies in   wu.cgi   and can be summarized as follows:  
 
  UTA0576 submits a Perl script with a   .zip   extension to the  wu.cgi     upload handler.  
  The handler calculates the MD5 hash of the filename supplied by the client and writes the uploaded content to   /home/runtime/tmp/<MD5(filename)>  .  
  Only after writing the file to disk does  wu.cgi     check whether it is a valid ZIP. The Perl script fails this check, causing the handler to delete it. However, the file exists on disk for a short period before that deletion.  
  The attacker exploits this window by sending parallel requests with the header   X-DSCGI-PATH: /home/runtime/tmp/<MD5(filename)>  , using the same technique described in the previous step to execute the uploaded script.  
  The race condition is between execution and deletion: if an execution request reaches the uploaded script before  wu.cgi     deletes it, the attacker’s code runs. Sending several execution requests in quick succession increases the likelihood of reaching the file during this window.  
 
 During this activity, UTA0576 used this exploit to upload and execute a Perl script, which executes a Bash script that in turn executes a Python script. The Python script is delivered in a Base64-encoded, zlib-compressed format. Once the Python script is decompressed and decoded, it is executed via  exec() , meaning the raw script is only ever stored in memory. 
 Ivanti is tracking both the RCE and authentication bypass components of this chain under CVE-2026-104935. This vulnerability was fixed in patches released on October 13, 2026. 
 Privilege Escalation Exploit and Anti-forensics 
 As detailed so far, the exploit chain gives UTA0576 access to code execution in the context of the  cgi-server  user. The threat actor then chained a separate privilege escalation exploit to gain access to root privileges. This exploit was passed via the in-memory Python script executed by the RCE Perl script. The high-level details of this exploit are outlined below: 
 
 ICS VPN appliances run a privileged background service named  dsinvoked , which runs maintenance tasks as root on demand. 
 The  dsinvoked  service looks up which program each task runs in  DSCache , a shared ICS configuration store. 
 UTA0576 patches the  cgi-server  process’s in-memory copy of the Ivanti library  /home/lib/libdsplibs.so , allowing it to modify  DSCache  and reconfigure an existing maintenance task to launch the Perl interpreter instead of its legitimate script. 
 The exploit code then requests that  dsinvoked  run the task, supplying a malicious Perl script as the argument;  dsinvoked  executes the script as root. 
 The exploit script checks for successful root-level access by checking whether  /etc/shadow  is readable. 
 After root-level execution has been achieved, UTA0576’s exploit script restores the in-memory  DSCache  entry to the legitimate, pre-exploitation script and restores the  libdsplibs.so  library to its pre-exploitation state. 
 The exploit code then removes log entries relating to the exploitation from the following targeted Ivanti runtime and Linux audit logs:
 
     /home/runtime/dlogs/debuglog  
     /var/log/audit/audit.log  
 
 
 
 For each command executed by UTA0576, the entire exploit chain is executed. The result of each command is then returned via the HTTP response. Volexity did not identify first-stage malware or web shells that would have enabled the threat actor to execute commands without re-exploiting the ICS VPN appliance. 
 Ivanti publishes an  Integrity Checker Tool  to identify unexpected file modifications on disk. However, because this exploit chain patches library code in memory only and restores configuration store data, the tool does not detect any modifications. As such, forensic investigation is required to identify evidence of exploitation. 
 Ivanti is working on a fix for the privilege escalation vulnerability, and it will be included in a future release in the coming weeks. 
 Post-exploitation Activity 
 Through forensic analysis, Volexity identified numerous post-exploitation activities undertaken by UTA0576. Volexity assesses with high confidence that UTA0576 was actively interacting with the results of their commands rather than simply executing a post-exploitation script. This is based on the diversity of approaches and commands executed. 
 Based on Volexity’s observations, UTA0576 primarily focused on credential theft, data exfiltration, log tampering, and network reconnaissance. Each of these is further detailed in the sections that follow. 
 Active Directory and Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) 
 UTA0576 gained access to Active Directory and then used this access to run queries and export results to JSON files in  /tmp/  for exfiltration. Based on filenames, commands, and cleanup actions, Volexity assesses with high confidence that UTA0576 exfiltrated information that could be queried from the target’s Active Directory. 
 UTA0576 also used a custom LDAPv3 tool and accompanying malicious Python script, writing them to  /tmp/ml.py  and  /tmp/rq5.py . This authenticated to an internal domain controller via LDAP using the ICS VPN appliance’s Active Directory service account and searched for high-value Active Directory attributes. These included the following: 
 
 Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) credentials 
 BitLocker recovery information 
 Active Directory attributes containing  userPassword  and  unixUserPassword  values 
 Logon script paths and other user account metadata 
 
 The results of this search were written to zlib-compressed, Base64-encoded JSON files stored in  /tmp/ . These files were exfiltrated via the exploit channel. 
 LDAP Packet Capture 
 Volexity identified a command that executed a packet parsing tool configured to filter for packets on TCP port 389 (commonly used for LDAP). This tool parsed a file stored at  /data/.icscap/cap0 . Volexity also observed logs showing that UTA0576 exfiltrated raw packet capture file data. 
 Volexity assesses with high confidence that UTA0576 was attempting to extract credentials from LDAP traffic by inspecting an existing packet capture file on the ICS VPN appliance. UTA0576 first attempted to parse the capture locally, filtering for TCP port 389 traffic, and then attempted to exfiltrate the first 8 KB of the file. It is worth noting that this technique was also recently used by another threat actor, which Volexity tracks as UTA0533,  who obtained root access via zero-day exploitation on SonicWall SMA VPN appliances . 
 UTA0576 wrote  /data/.icscap/h.py  to disk and executed it using  /home/venv3/bin/python3.6  during their operation. Analysis of  h.py  revealed its main functionality is to parse packet captures stored in  /data/.icscap/cap*   to harvest plaintext LDAP credentials, HTTP Basic Authentication credentials, and NTLM challenge-response hashes. It prints recovered credentials and password-cracking material to standard output, allowing the attacker to collect authentication data from intercepted network traffic. 
 UTA0576 wrote a Python implementation of Kerberos to  /tmp/mk.py  and an accompanying malicious script to  /tmp/rr.py . The  mk.py  script handles basic Kerberos tests, which  rr.py  used to test credentials. Volexity noted that  mk.py  also contained  Kerberoast  functionality that was not used by the  rr.py  script. 
 Ivanti Connect Secure Configuration and Authentication Log Reconnaissance 
 UTA0576 sought to exfiltrate configuration and authentication data used by the compromised ICS VPN appliance. Targeted files and directories included the following: 
 
     /home/etc/pulse/  
   /home/etc/  
   /home/*.cfg   
   /home/runtime  
 
 UTA0576 also sought to parse local authentication logs to steal credentials from the compromised ICS VPN appliance. Volexity observed evidence of the following actions undertaken by the attacker: 
 
 Attempted username extraction from  log.events.vc0  with results written to  /tmp/pu.txt  
 Extensive grep searching for authentication events and logs 
 
 Network Reconnaissance and Password Spraying 
 UTA0576 exfiltrated the contents of  /etc/resolv.conf  and ran network resolution for various internal domains belonging to the targeted organization. The threat actor then used a Python helper script,  sp_run.py , to conduct a series of password-spraying attacks against Active Directory accounts. The following files related to this activity were written to  /tmp/  and exfiltrated: 
 
    sp_out.txt  
  spray_hits.json  
 
 Anti-Forensics and Cleanup 
 Volexity’s analysis of UTA0576’s payloads recovered from the ICS VPN appliance identified several anti-forensic capabilities designed to remove evidence of exploitation, conceal privileged execution, and reduce residual artifacts: 
 
  Log tampering:  The payload selectively removes recent entries from  /home/runtime/dlogs/debuglog  and  /var/log/audit/audit.log . It reads both logs, filters entries within the targeted time window, and truncates and rewrites the files with the remaining records. This preserves older entries while attempting to remove evidence of malicious activity. 
  Payload self-deletion:  The root-stage Perl payload attempts to unlink its own execution file ( /home/runtime/tmp/ics-root-run-inband-*.pl ) after execution begins. The preceding Python stage also attempts to delete the script during cleanup. 
  Temporary file cleanup:  The payload removes temporary execution results ( /home/runtime/tmp/ics-root-result-inband-* ) and attempts to delete the original CGI source and temporary gate file. 
  Additional script removal:  Recovered commands explicitly delete  /tmp/rq5.py  and  /tmp/rr.py  using  rm -f  after executing the LDAP and Kerberos helper scripts. 
  Privilege-escalation cleanup:  After obtaining root execution, the payload restores the  DSCache ScriptUtil/updateOpswatSDK  command to  /home/bin/updateOpswatSDK.pl , removing the temporary redirection to the Perl interpreter. 
  Memory patch restoration:  The payload restores the modified instruction byte in its own process memory through  /proc/self/mem , removing the temporary patch associated with the privilege-escalation mechanism. The on-disk library is not modified. 
  Output suppression:  Background cleanup processes redirect standard input, output, and error streams to  /dev/null , reducing visible execution artifacts and error messages. 
  Tool masquerading and capture rotation:  The attacker used a renamed  tcpdump  executable ( /data/.icscap/dsstatmond ) and eight rotating packet-capture files. Earlier captured traffic was overwritten as the capture buffer rotated. 
 
 The recovered payloads demonstrate deliberate efforts to conceal malicious activity through selective log modification, removal of temporary execution artifacts, and restoration of altered system state. Although these capabilities are confirmed in the recovered code, the extent to which each operation completed successfully on the compromised ICS VPN appliance has not been fully established. 
 Attribution 
 Volexity assesses with low confidence that UTA0576 has criminal, rather than espionage, motivations based on the target of this activity. The host used for this operation,  108.165.147[.]64 , is an  Evoxt VPS  and was observed running an OpenVPN server from September 30 to October 7, 2026. 
 Ivanti Memory Analysis with Volexity Volcano 
 For its investigation, Volexity relied heavily on memory analysis with  Volcano  to detect and respond to this zero-day exploitation. Volcano ships with various indicators of compromise (IOCs) that can flag suspicious activity in analyzed evidence, which is summarized on the  Alerts  tab.    The following screenshot, taken directly from Volcano’s  Alerts  tab by a Volexity incident responder during the investigation, immediately shows evidence of attacker activity: 
   
 The first two alerts point directly to the network sniffer used by the exploit chain and its operator. The “Linux Socket Filters” indicator reports that  dsstatmond  (PID 5012) is sniffing network traffic. Given the role and network placement of the ICS VPN appliance, packets that traverse its interfaces contain a significant amount of sensitive information. Network sniffing is a common technique deployed against compromised edge and core networking devices analyzed by Volexity. In fact, the same Volcano IOC also triggers on the well-known  BPFDoor  because its packet sniffer leverages BPF filters. 
 Pivoting from the “Commands from Hidden Directories” alert brings Volcano Viewer to the process table, as shown below: 
   
 The  dsstatmond  process is running from a directory named  .icscap  for stealth, which is in fact hidden from normal file system listings. Based on the command-line parameters, the BPF/PCAP filter only records traffic on network ports used by common plaintext protocols, such as LDAP, HTTP, FTP, and telnet. Sniffing on these ports allows for direct capture of sensitive information, such as credentials, administrator commands, and file transfer contents as mentioned earlier. 
 Volcano also recovers files and file system activity from memory for comprehensive analysis. As shown in the following screenshot, many of the tools and exploit chain components are recoverable from memory, including output JSON files, Python scripts, and the PCAP files created by  dsstatmond : 
   
 The open file descriptor path  /home/root/data/.icscap/cap6  corroborates the process command line value. 
 These examples provide just a glimpse of how Volcano’s memory analysis capability exposes volatile artifacts – even on edge devices and  especially  when attackers are engaging in anti-forensics tactics. 
 Conclusion 
 In this blog post, Volexity outlined three zero-day exploits in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances which, when chained together, grant unauthenticated root-privilege RCE. These exploits affect versions up to 22.8R2.4, Build 19097, which at the time of writing is the latest version. Volexity reported these exploits and their abuse to Ivanti as part of a coordinated disclosure process. Ivanti is releasing a patch for the authentication bypass and RCE vulnerability (CVE-2026-104935) on the October 13, 2026; Ivanti is working on a fix for the privilege escalation vulnerability which will be patched in a future release. 
 Volexity’s forensic investigation revealed that, immediately after exploiting an ICS VPN appliance, UTA0576 began conducting reconnaissance, stealing credentials, and exfiltrating data. Because the operation was detected and disrupted, the threat actor’s ultimate objectives could not be determined. However, Volexity assesses with high confidence that UTA0576’s actions signaled preparation for lateral movement and a broader compromise of the victim network. 
 As with many other threat actor operations Volexity has investigated in 2026, Volexity assesses with medium confidence that UTA0576 makes use of large language models (LLMs) for exploit development and post-exploitation activity. This assessment is based on the continuous use of the exploit channel to pass commands to the compromised host (rather than a simpler method such as a web shell), the repeated deployment of highly specific scripts using hardcoded credentials (rather than generic pre-built utilities), and the complexity of the exploit chain. 
 To generally prevent these attacks, Volexity recommends the following: 
 
 Apply the patches for affected devices  published by Ivanti . 
 Monitor for large numbers of network requests for  /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi . Malicious requests will use a header value similar to the following:
 
     X-DSCGI-PATH: /home/webserver/htdocs/dana/fb/smb/wu.cgi  
   X-DSCGI-PATH: /home/runtime/tmp/<MD5(filename)>  
 
 
 It is likely that threat actors will identify additional paths that can either be used as the URL or header target for this exploit. If possible, monitoring for mismatches between the URL path and  X-DSCGI-PATH  is advisable. 
 Check the  /tmp/  directory for evidence of post-exploitation actions. 
 If you suspect your device has been compromised, conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of exploitation. The Ivanti Integrity Checker may not be able to identify device compromise. 
 Upgrade ICS VPN appliances running any of the following versions to the newest version:
 
 25.1.1 and prior 
 25.1.2 
 22.8R2.4 
 
 
 
 Related indicators can be downloaded from the  Volexity GitHub page .

      Title: Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories 
      Authors:  Ali Behrouz ,  Farnoosh Hashemi ,  Adel Javanmard ,  Vahab Mirrokni               View a PDF of the paper titled Language Models Need Sleep: Learning to Self-Modify and Consolidate Memories, by Ali Behrouz and Farnoosh Hashemi and Adel Javanmard and Vahab Mirrokni 
     View PDF 
     HTML (experimental) 



     
             Abstract: The past few decades have witnessed significant advances in the design of machine learning algorithms, from early studies on task-specific shallow models to more general deep Large Language Models (LLMs). Despite showing promising results in tasks that require instant prediction or in-context learning, existing models lack the ability to continually learn and effectively transfer their temporal in-context knowledge to their long-term parameters. Inspired by human learning process, we introduce a ''Sleep'' paradigm that allows the models to continually learn, distill their short-term fragile memories into stable long-term knowledge with replay, and recursively improve themselves with ''Dreaming'' process. In more detail, sleep consists of two stages: (1) Memory Consolidation: an upward distillation process, called Knowledge Seeding, where the memories of a smaller-self are distilled into a larger network to provide more capacity while preserving the knowledge. As a proof of concept, we present a new Generalized Distillation process for {Knowledge Seeding} (i.e., the combination of on-policy distillation with Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based imitation learning); (2) Dreaming: a self-improvement phase, where the model uses RL to generate a curriculum of synthetic data to rehearse new knowledge and refine existing capabilities without human supervision. Our experiments on long-horizon, continual learning, knowledge incorporation, and few-shot generalization tasks support the importance of the sleep stage.

         The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning 

        

           
              October 27, 2026    Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni, Google Research  
           

        

         
          
         
     
   
 


     
         
             
                
                     
                        
                        

 
    
 

 
     We introduce a sleep phase in continual learning, enabling large language models to continuously integrate new facts and enhance reasoning while mitigating catastrophic forgetting or static knowledge cutoffs. 
 
                        
                     
                
                
                 
                    
                 

                 
                    
                    
    


 
     
        
  


 
  




   Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and  in-context learning  (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information.  While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger  catastrophic forgetting , a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten.  Inspired by how the human brain processes and stabilizes memory during rest, we introduce a  sleep framework  in continual learning: a learning paradigm that equips large language models (LLMs) with a continuous  periodic  lifecycle, enabling them to continually learn, consolidate fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. With this framework, we demonstrate that alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning. 
  
 


     
 

                    
                    
    


 
     
        
  


 
  




   Rethinking machine learning: Active (wake) vs. sleep phases  Traditional machine learning relies on a strict separation between training and inference. In a continual learning framework, this distinction becomes artificial; an intelligent agent must constantly learn, adapt, and process information.  Under the sleep paradigm, an LLM operates across two primary states:    Active (wake) phase : The model actively receives, processes, and interacts with inputs, storing temporary information in fast, short-term memory components.   Sleep phase : The model pauses processing new inputs and redirects its internal computations toward memory consolidation and self-improvement.   While terms like "sleep," "dreaming," and "self-improvement" borrow from neuroscience, our framework operates entirely within a fixed model architecture and human-defined training rules. During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples. This automated post-training cycle helps a deployed model absorb new facts and sharpen its reasoning accuracy while keeping its core codebase and design unchanged. 
  
 


     
 

                    
                    
    


 
     
        
  


 
  




   Key components of the sleep process  The sleep paradigm addresses catastrophic forgetting and continuous adaptation through two stages: memory consolidation and dreaming.  1. Memory consolidation  In the human brain,  non-rapid eye movement  (NREM) slow-wave sleep consolidates fragile memories into long-term structures via abstraction and distillation. Our proposed sleep framework mirrors this natural phenomenon through two key technical mechanisms:    Parameter expansion & continuum memory hierarchy:  To prevent catastrophic forgetting, the model dynamically scales its capacity during sleep. Using a  Mixture of Experts  (MoE) and  Hope  architecture , newly unlocked, low-rank experts are integrated into stable, lower-frequency memory blocks to store incoming knowledge without disrupting older parameters.   Knowledge seeding (upward distillation):  Fragile short-term memories stored in high-frequency layers (e.g., in-context memory) are transferred into the newly expanded long-term parameters. This is achieved through  Generalized Knowledge Distillation  (GKD) combined with  reinforcement learning  (RL)-based  imitation learning :   On-policy distillation:  The expanded student model learns token-specific feedback from teacher distributions generated on self-sampled sequences.   Learning to imitate (LTI):  The student model is rewarded based on semantic and absolute similarity ( Levenshtein distance ) when completing prefixes of teacher-generated text.     Synaptic pruning:  Once the memory consolidation into lower-frequency modules is complete, the high-frequency temporary parameters are reset, freeing up capacity for future active sessions.  
  
 


     
 

                    
                    
    


 
     
        
  


  

   

    




     
      
         
           
            



  
    





     
    
        
    


 


 
    
    
         
    
     
    
 
  


           
         
      

      
         
            Overview of our sleep framework: Input streams from the active phase are stored in short-term memory before entering the sleep cycle, which bifurcates into Consolidation (transferring fragile short-term tokens into expanded long-term parametric memory using low-rank structures and MoE) and Dreaming (autonomous self-improvement via synthetic routing with random experts and RL refinement).  
         
      
     
   



     
 

                    
                    
    


 
     
        
  


 
  




   2. Dreaming for self-improvement  During  REM sleep , the human brain actively simulates scenarios, consolidates emotional/semantic connections, and explores novel neural pathways. Mirroring this, during the “dreaming stage”, the sleep framework implements an autonomous self-improvement loop:    Random expert selection:  During synthetic data generation, the MoE router randomly activates non-standard experts. This forces the model to mix disparate domains of knowledge and uncover latent patterns.   Curated rehearsal:  The model generates synthetic training samples ("dreams") and filters them using gradient-based data selection to prioritize samples with the highest potential to boost overall model capability.   RL refinement:  The model performs supervised fine-tuning on top-rated dream samples and evaluates whether the generation improves performance on downstream tasks.  
  
 


     
 

                    
                    
    


 
     
        
  


 
  




   Theoretical foundations  Beyond the empirical results, our sleep paradigm is grounded in a theory that clarifies why its two stages (memory consolidation and dreaming) can support continual learning without simply trading new knowledge for old capabilities.  For memory consolidation, the analysis shows that knowledge seeding can be understood as a structured, low-rank compression problem. The model is not asked to copy every detail of its short-term traces into its parameters. Instead, it identifies a compact set of directions that best preserve both the model’s own on-policy behavior and the semantic qualities rewarded by the learning objective.  This perspective explains the complementary roles of the two signals: on-policy distillation aligns consolidation with the trajectories the model will actually produce at inference time, reducing the mismatch that can arise when training only on teacher-generated distributions; meanwhile, the semantic reward changes what is worth retaining, prioritizing directions that preserve meaning and task-relevant behavior rather than merely matching token probabilities. Parameter expansion then provides the capacity needed to write these selected memories without overwriting previously consolidated knowledge.  For dreaming, the theory characterizes random expert activation and reward-based sample selection as mechanisms for improving the geometry of learning. Injecting different MoEs broadens the set of gradient directions explored during synthetic generation, exposing the model to a richer collection of updates than those induced by its ordinary wake-time data alone. Gradient-based filtering then emphasizes the synthetic experiences that carry the most useful learning signal, strengthening informative directions while preserving the structure of the underlying gradient space.  Together, these steps yield a more balanced optimization landscape: learning is less dominated by a small number of directions, gradients are better conditioned, and the model can make more stable progress when refining its capabilities. In this view, dreaming is not simply self-generated data augmentation; it is a deliberate process for diversifying, selecting, and consolidating the updates through which the model improves itself. 
  
 


     
 

                    
                    
    


 
     
        
  


  

   

    




     
      
         
           
            



  
    





     
    
        
    


 


 
    
    
         
    
     
    
 
  


           
         
      

      
         
            Comparative performance of our sleep framework against baseline approaches (such as in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning) across major evaluation axes, including Class-Incremental Learning, continual translation, long-context scaling up to 10M tokens, factual knowledge incorporation, and mathematical reasoning.  
         
      
     
   



     
 

                    
                    
    


 
     
        
  


 
  




   For  continual translation , in unseen languages, such as Manchu and Kalamang, the sleep framework maintained a near-zero performance drop in multi-stage evaluations, whereas standard baselines like ICL,  Cartridges , and  supervised fine-tuning  (SFT) suffered severe catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning.  In long-context understanding on the  BABILong  benchmark, our sleep method demonstrated near-perfect scaling up to 10M tokens, outperforming strong baselines like  GPT-4 , and  Titans  by using sleep-time consolidation to compress long-context information directly into parametric memory.  For factual knowledge incorporation evaluated on  SQuAD  and  continued pre-training  (CPT), our sleep method achieved 48.9% on single-task and 46.2% on CPT evaluations, outperforming baseline methods including the base model, SFT, and  Self-Adapting Language Models  (SEAL) by successfully integrating new factual information without degrading existing model representations.  Finally, on mathematical reasoning benchmarks including  AIME 24/25  and  HMMT 25 , sleep-enhanced base-model achieved accuracy scores of 79.2%, 69.0%, and 46.1%, respectively. This outperformed baselines like SFT, group relative policy optimization (GRPO), and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), showing that pairing memory consolidation with imitation learning drives superior reasoning performance. 
  
 


     
 

                    
                    
    


 
     
        
  


 
  




   Conclusion  Our sleep paradigm provides a path toward autonomous, continually learning AI systems. By moving beyond static pre-training and fragile context windows, alternating between active learning and offline rest empowers LLMs to retain short-term memories, abstract new skills into long-term parameter structures, and continuously self-improve without catastrophic forgetting. 
  
 


     
 

                    
                    
    


 
     
        
  


 
  




   Acknowledgements    This research    was conducted by Ali Behrouz (Google and Cornell University), Farnoosh Hashemi (Cornell University), Adel Javanmard (Google and University of Southern California), and Vahab Mirrokni. We thank Yuan Deng and Corinna Cortes for reviewing the work and their valuable suggestions. We also thank Mark Simborg, Kimberly Schwede, and Tim Herrmann for their help in crafting this blog post.

Lightpanda Browser

The headless browser built from scratch for AI agents and automation.
Not a Chromium fork. Not a WebKit patch. A new browser, written in Zig.
16x lighter and 9x faster than Chromium.

[![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/lightpanda-io/browser)](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/blob/main/LICENSE) [![Twitter Follow](https://img.shields.io/twitter/follow/lightpanda_io)](https://twitter.com/lightpanda_io) [![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/lightpanda-io/browser)](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/discord/1391984864894521354?style=flat-square&label=discord)](https://discord.gg/K63XeymfB5)
[ ](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/demo)   [ ](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/demo)
## Benchmarks Requesting 933 real web pages over the network on a AWS EC2 m5.large instance. See [benchmark details](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/demo/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md#crawler-benchmark). | Metric | Lightpanda | Headless Chrome | Difference | | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | | Memory (peak, 100 pages) | 123MB | 2GB | ~16x less | | Execution time (100 pages) | 5s | 46s | ~9x faster | ## Quick start ### Install **Package Managers** Latest nightly from Homebrew: ```console brew install lightpanda-io/browser/lightpanda ``` Latest nightly from Arch Linux User Repository: ```console yay -S lightpanda-nightly-bin ``` **Download from the nightly builds** You can download the last binary from the [nightly builds](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/releases/tag/nightly) for Linux and MacOS for both x86_64 and aarch64. *For Linux* ```console curl -L -o lightpanda https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/releases/download/nightly/lightpanda-x86_64-linux && \ chmod a+x ./lightpanda ``` Verify the binary before running anything: ```console ./lightpanda version ``` [Linux aarch64 is also available](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/releases/tag/nightly) If you use [**Nix**](https://nixos.org/download/), you can run Lightpanda directly from the flake without downloading a binary: ```console nix run github:lightpanda-io/browser -- --help ``` Or pin it as an input in your own flake: ```nix { inputs.lightpanda.url = "github:lightpanda-io/browser"; } ``` > **Note:** The Linux release binaries are linked against glibc. On musl-based Linux distributions (Alpine, etc.) the binary fails with `cannot execute: required file not found` because the glibc dynamic linker is missing. Use a glibc-based base image (e.g., `FROM debian:bookworm-slim` or `FROM ubuntu:24.04`) or [build from sources](#build-from-sources). > > **Android / Termux:** there is no native Android build. The Linux aarch64 binary needs the glibc loader (`/lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1`), which Android's Bionic libc does not provide, so it fails with the same `cannot execute: required file not found` error. *For MacOS* ```console curl -L -o lightpanda https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/releases/download/nightly/lightpanda-aarch64-macos && \ chmod a+x ./lightpanda ``` [MacOS x86_64 is also available](https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/releases/tag/nightly) *For Windows + WSL2* Lightpanda has no native Windows binary. Install it inside WSL following the Linux steps above. WSL not installed? Run `wsl --install` from an administrator shell, restart, then open `wsl`. See [Microsoft's WSL install guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install) for details. Your automation client (Puppeteer, Playwright, etc.) can run either inside WSL or on the Windows host. WSL forwards `localhost:9222` automatically. **Install from Docker** Lightpanda provides [official Docker images](https://hub.docker.com/r/lightpanda/browser) for both Linux amd64 and arm64 architectures. The following command fetches the Docker image and starts a new container exposing Lightpanda's CDP server on port `9222`. ```console docker run -d --name lightpanda -p 127.0.0.1:9222:9222 lightpanda/browser:latest ``` ### Dump a URL ```console ./lightpanda fetch --obey-robots --dump html --log-format pretty --log-level info https://demo-browser.lightpanda.io/campfire-commerce/ ``` You can use `--dump markdown` to convert directly into markdown, or `--dump png > page.png` or `--dump pdf > page.pdf` for a text-only rendering of the page. `--dump structured_data` prints the page's JSON-LD, OpenGraph, Twitter card, meta and link tags as JSON, like the MCP `structuredData` tool. `--wait-until`, `--wait-ms`, `--wait-selector` and `--wait-script` are available to adjust waiting time before dump. ### Start a CDP server ```console ./lightpanda serve --obey-robots --log-format pretty --log-level info --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9222 ``` To listen on a Unix-domain socket (owner-only, mode 0600) instead of TCP: ```console ./lightpanda serve --unix-socket /run/user/1000/lightpanda.sock ``` Once the CDP server started, you can run a Puppeteer script by configuring the `browserWSEndpoint`.
Example Puppeteer script ```js import puppeteer from 'puppeteer-core'; // use browserWSEndpoint to pass the Lightpanda's CDP server address. const browser = await puppeteer.connect({ browserWSEndpoint: "ws://127.0.0.1:9222", }); // The rest of your script remains the same. const context = await browser.createBrowserContext(); const frame = await context.newPage(); // Dump all the links from the frame. await frame.goto('https://demo-browser.lightpanda.io/amiibo/', {waitUntil: "networkidle0"}); const links = await frame.evaluate(() => { return Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('a')).map(row => { return row.getAttribute('href'); }); }); console.log(links); await frame.close(); await context.close(); await browser.disconnect(); ```
#### Start a webdriver Bidi server Use `--protocol webdriver` to enable Bidi support. You can start both, CDP and Bidi, with `--protocol webdriver --protocol cdp` ```console ./lightpanda serve --obey-robots --log-format pretty --log-level info --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9222 --protocol webdriver ``` ### Agent mode `lightpanda agent` lets you drive the browser with a native agent. Describe what you want in plain English or with slash commands, and it controls the browser: navigating pages, clicking through flows, filling forms, extracting structured data. Think of it as a robot you're directing to use the web, more than a chatbot you're having a conversation with. Because the agent runs inside the same process as the browser, every tool call is a direct operation and you retain Lightpanda's speed and memory advantage. The output of an agent session is a [PandaScript](https://lightpanda.io/docs/usage/pandascript): vanilla JavaScript with a small set of native browser primitives built directly into Lightpanda. Run `/save` to export one from your current session, then replay it with `lightpanda run
