# OpenMausBot **The open-source Grok Bot alternative: your own team of AI bots, in a chat app.** [**openmausbot.com**](https://www.openmausbot.com)  ·  [Download](https://www.openmausbot.com/download)  ·  [Open source Grok Bot alternative, compared](https://www.openmausbot.com/blog/grok-bot-vs-openmausbot) OpenMausBot is an open-source Grok Bot alternative: an independent project inspired by **Grok Bot**, and the open-source alternative to **Meta Muse**, **OpenAI dots** and **Cue by Manus** — bring-your-own-agent, local-first, on the models you already have. Also known as **MausBot**; formerly **OpenGrokBot**. Not affiliated with xAI, Meta, OpenAI or Manus. Every bot in the sidebar is a real agent — Claude or Codex running locally under the hood — with its own personality, its own model, its own cloud computer, and its own connected apps. Talk to them like contacts. Watch them work. Approve what matters. ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-strict-3178C6?logo=typescript&logoColor=white) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-19-61DAFB?logo=react&logoColor=black) ![Electron](https://img.shields.io/badge/Electron-macOS%20%C2%B7%20Windows%20%C2%B7%20Ubuntu-2B2E3A?logo=electron&logoColor=9FEAF9) ![Agents](https://img.shields.io/badge/agents-Claude%20·%20Codex-d97757) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/milind-soni/OpenMausBot?label=release&color=1084fe&cacheSeconds=300)](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/releases/latest) ![PRs](https://img.shields.io/badge/PRs-welcome-38d591)
      [latest release](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/releases/latest)  ·  macOS: Apple silicon & Intel · signed & notarized .dmg  ·  Windows: x64 installer  ·  Ubuntu 24.04 x64: .deb or AppImage beta  ·  [all releases](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/releases)


Powered by boat.dev


--- > ⚠️ **No affiliation with any cryptocurrency.** OpenMausBot has no token. Any coin using the OpenMausBot, Maus, or SupaMaus name is not created, endorsed, or affiliated with this project or its maintainer. I have received no tokens, payment, or allocation from anyone, and I will not be endorsing any token. ## Why One assistant in one box is the wrong shape for agents. OpenMausBot is an independent, open-source project inspired by **Grok Bot** — it keeps the idea (AI as a *messaging app*: a roster of bots you chat with, each with its own personality, memory of its thread, model, computer, and apps) and rebuilds it open, local-first, and on the agents you already have: - **Bring your own agents.** Bots run on the `claude`, `codex`, and `grok` CLIs installed on your own machine — your existing logins and subscriptions, no new accounts, no proxy in the middle. Point any engine at a custom CLI binary (a versioned build or wrapper) in **Settings → Engines**. - **Local first.** One small harness server on `127.0.0.1` owns every agent process. Transcripts, keys, and events live in `~/.openmausbot`, not a cloud. - **Agents with hands.** Each bot can use a cloud Linux desktop, an isolated Local VM, or—where the platform safety boundary is currently certified—your own computer, plus 500+ apps through Composio. Host control is available on macOS and Ubuntu Xorg after explicit opt-in. Ubuntu Wayland host control remains disabled while issue #345 is resolved. ## The open-source alternative to Grok Bot, Muse, dots and Cue Four closed personal-agent products shipped in seven weeks of 2026, and each one keeps the model, the computer and your data on its maker's side of the line. OpenMausBot is the open-source version of that shape: a team of agents in a chat app, each with its own model, its own computer and its own connected apps, running on your machine under Apache 2.0. If you searched for an *open Muse*, *open dots*, an *open-source Grok Bot*, an *open Instinct* or an *open Cue*, this is the repository. | Looking for | What it is | How OpenMausBot differs | Read more | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Open source Grok Bot** | xAI's roster of bots on one shared cloud computer, Grok only, from a SuperGrok or Cursor plan | Same roster shape; any model per bot; your own machine; approval cards | [Grok Bot vs OpenMausBot](https://www.openmausbot.com/blog/grok-bot-vs-openmausbot) | | **Open Muse** | Meta's single personal agent in a Meta cloud VM, US and Canada only | A team instead of one agent; runs anywhere; data in `~/.openmausbot` | [Meta Muse alternative](https://www.openmausbot.com/blog/open-source-alternative-to-meta-muse) | | **Open dots** | OpenAI's always-on agent inside ChatGPT, GPT only, Pro and Business Premium plans | Several agents; your Claude, ChatGPT or Grok login; no plan required | [OpenAI dots alternative](https://www.openmausbot.com/blog/openai-dots-alternative) | | **Open Cue** | Manus's invite-only agents with their own phone, email and wallet | No invite; OAuth instead of passwords; open source | [Cue by Manus alternative](https://www.openmausbot.com/blog/open-source-alternative-to-cue-by-manus) | | **Open Instinct** | Spear Street's invite-only agent that holds your passwords on a cloud computer | Ask for approval when you want it; signs in over OAuth; your machine | [Instinct AI alternative](https://www.openmausbot.com/blog/instinct-ai-alternative) | All five side by side: [Muse vs Grok Bot vs Dots vs Cue](https://www.openmausbot.com/blog/muse-vs-grok-bot-vs-dots-vs-cue), and a decision guide in five questions: [Which AI agent should I use?](https://www.openmausbot.com/blog/which-ai-agent-should-i-use) ## Features
### 🧠 Pick a brain per bot A model picker with a provider rail — Claude and Codex models side by side, defaults marked, unavailable providers dimmed with the reason. Switch a bot's model mid-conversation. ### 🖥️ Every bot gets a computer Open the Computer panel and the bot's cloud desktop spins up on its own — live screen preview while it works, "Open desktop" to take over in your browser, or point the bot at *this Mac* instead.
### 🙋 Bots ask before they act Shell commands, file edits, and questions surface as inline cards — Allow / Deny / answer in chat. A permission broker turns every risky action into a decision you make, for cloud and local computers alike. ### 🔌 Connected apps A one-click marketplace over Composio Sessions: Gmail, Slack, GitHub, Notion, Linear and hundreds more. OAuth once, and every bot can use them as tools.
### 🗂 Manage bots like chats Right-click any bot: pin, mark unread, edit profile, duplicate, copy conversation ID, hide, delete. It's a messaging app — your agents behave like contacts. ### 🔑 Keys once, everything lights up Paste credentials in App Settings — they persist locally and the provider fleet hot-reloads instantly. Secrets are write-only: the UI only ever sees "configured" flags.
### #️⃣ Channels for every context Keep Work, Personal, and each project in separate channels without cloning your bots. Every channel has its own transcript, shared instructions, working folder, responder rules, and editable bot roster. File a channel and its bots under a named context, then rename it or change its members whenever the team changes. ### ⚡ Fast decisions with Jev Add a TypeSafe Jev key, or an OpenRouter key and model, in **Settings → Decision model** and rooms set to **Auto** pick the bot that fits each un-mentioned message in a few hundred milliseconds, falling back to the room's lead whenever the decision model is off or unsure. See [docs/decision-model.md](docs/decision-model.md). ### 📦 Install a complete team from one Markdown file Browse outcome-driven teams on [BotMRR](https://botmrr.io), then choose **Add to OpenMausBot**. The app opens a review screen before creating the bots, Chief of Staff, channels, playbooks, connector checklist, and suggested routines. You can also import the same `.md` file from disk or paste its public GitHub URL in **Teams → Import**. The format stays portable: OpenMausBot reads the structured YAML frontmatter for a reliable one-click install, while Grok, Claude, ChatGPT, and people can follow the ordinary Markdown playbook. Connections remain off until you approve them, routines arrive paused, and packages never carry credentials, conversations, permissions, memory, or computer access. Browse the [open-source playbook repository](https://github.com/milind-soni/openmausbot-teams) or read its [portable format](https://github.com/milind-soni/openmausbot-teams/blob/main/FORMAT.md). ### 🤝 Share a whole department Right-click a department and choose **Share department…** (or use **Templates → Share**) to save the whole department as one file: its bots with their instructions, pictures and skills, group chats, routines, shared instructions, Chief of Staff, connection slots and each bot's starter notes (untick them to leave them out). The dialog shows exactly what the file holds before you save it. Chat history, keys and passwords, model choices and computers never go in, and anything that looks like a secret is removed from the text. Whoever imports it gets new bots on Ask, skills switched off and routines paused. See [docs/team-sharing.md](docs/team-sharing.md). Desktops connected to an organization also get **Templates → From {Organization}**: the packages its Admin shares, added with one click, skills switched on. See [docs/org-library.md](docs/org-library.md). Your New bot defaults can travel too, as a **preset bot** that appears in New bot (in a team file, or on their own with **Share as preset…**). See [docs/presets.md](docs/presets.md). ### 🎧 Bots that talk back Press the speaker on any reply, or switch a bot to read its answers out as they land — so you can listen to what ran overnight while you make breakfast. Hit **call** and it's a conversation: it hears you, tells you what it's doing while it works, and asks for approvals out loud. Choose ElevenLabs, Fish Audio, Grok (xAI), built-in Mac voices, or a local Chatterbox server in an agent profile. Paste a cloud key once when needed, pick a voice, and every bot can talk. Give a bot its own voice and a channel stops sounding like one person. For Grok, save your xAI API key in **Settings → Connections**, then choose **Grok (xAI)** and a voice under the bot’s **Voice & alerts**. It reuses that host-side key and returns MP3 audio for spoken replies and calls. Language is detected automatically from the reply text; quality varies outside xAI’s [officially supported languages](https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/audio/text-to-speech). This adds speech synthesis to the existing call flow; microphone transcription remains unchanged. **Also in the box:** streaming replies with tool-run activity chips · native macOS dictation from the composer mic (on-device Apple speech recognition — desktop app) · SupaMaus cursor mascots with role-aware expressions · screenshots of the bot's work folded into the transcript. ## Powered By
![Claude](https://img.shields.io/badge/Claude-d97757?logo=claude&logoColor=white) ![Codex](https://img.shields.io/badge/Codex-000000) ![Grok](https://img.shields.io/badge/Grok%20CLI-000000?logo=x&logoColor=white) ![Electron](https://img.shields.io/badge/Electron-2B2E3A?logo=electron&logoColor=9FEAF9) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-20232A?logo=react&logoColor=61DAFB) ![Vite](https://img.shields.io/badge/Vite-646CFF?logo=vite&logoColor=white) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-0F172A?logo=tailwindcss&logoColor=38BDF8) ![Composio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Composio-e6493a) ![Boat](https://img.shields.io/badge/Boat-sponsor-111111) ![Cua](https://img.shields.io/badge/Cua%20Driver-1f2937) ![ElevenLabs](https://img.shields.io/badge/ElevenLabs-000000?logo=elevenlabs&logoColor=white) ![Fish Audio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Fish%20Audio-2563eb) ![GitHub Sponsors](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub%20Sponsors-ea4aaa)
| Service | Purpose | |---|---| | **Claude · Codex · Grok** | The agents behind every bot, run through their local CLIs | | **Electron** | Desktop shells for macOS, Windows, and Ubuntu | | **React + Vite + Tailwind CSS** | The chat app UI and its build | | **Boat** ([boat.dev](https://boat.dev)) | Each bot's cloud computer · our sponsor | | **Composio** | Connected apps — Gmail, Slack, GitHub, and more | | **Cua Driver** | Native computer use on your own machine | | **ElevenLabs · Fish Audio** | Hosted voices for bots that talk back | | **GitHub Sponsors** | One-time and monthly project support | ## How it works Two processes. The app holds no transports of its own — it sends typed commands over HTTP and folds one SSE event stream into state. The harness server owns every agent process and normalizes each provider's native protocol into one canonical runtime event stream (logged per-thread as NDJSON). ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph app ["App — React + Tailwind (5199)"] UI[Chat UI · model picker · computer panel] end subgraph server ["Harness server (127.0.0.1:8799)"] REG[Driver registry] --> BUS[Event bus → SSE] BROKER[Permission broker] end subgraph agents ["Agents on your computer"] CL[claude CLI] CX[codex CLI] GR[grok CLI] end UI -- "HTTP commands" --> server BUS -- "one SSE stream" --> UI REG --> CL & CX & GR CL & CX & GR -- "permission requests" --> BROKER server -- "Boat API" --> BOAT[("Cloud computer
boat.dev")] server -- "Composio Session" --> APPS[("Gmail · Slack · GitHub · …")] ``` | Layer | Where | What it does | |---|---|---| | Drivers | `server/drivers/` | One per provider: Claude, Codex, and Grok Build over their local CLIs (stream-JSON / JSON-RPC / ACP), plus a cloud-computer agent. Unknown drivers degrade to "unavailable", never crash the fleet. | | Harness | `server/harness/` | Registry (configs → live instances) and the fan-in event bus every client folds. | | API | `server/index.ts` | Bots, turns, approvals, model catalog, computer lifecycle, connectors, config — HTTP + SSE. | | Voice | `server/tts/` | ElevenLabs, Fish Audio, Grok (xAI), built-in Mac voices, or local Chatterbox. Cloud keys stay on the harness; markdown is rewritten into something worth hearing before it is spoken. | | App | `src/` | The chat shell. Server-backed store, one reducer, zero client-side transports. | | Desktop | `electron/` | macOS, Windows, and Ubuntu shells with an embedded harness and platform capabilities; Apple speech stays macOS-only, Ubuntu Xorg has opt-in local control, and Wayland remains fail-closed. | ### Orchestrate OpenMausBot over MCP OpenMausBot ships a stdio MCP server for external clients such as Claude Desktop and Cursor. It exposes a deliberately bounded team control plane: inspect bots and channels, read/search compact transcript pages, create and configure bots/channels/tasks, send work, wait for completion, switch models, and interrupt turns. It does **not** expose approval grants, deletion, arbitrary settings, credentials, or computer lifecycle. See [MCP server setup and tool reference](docs/mcp-server.md). ### Run it from scripts and CI The `openmausbot` command drives a running workspace without a screen: set a team up from a file, give a bot one job, wait until it and every teammate it asked are done, and export what they made. One JSON document with `--json`, and exit codes a script can branch on. ```sh openmausbot team apply team.yaml openmausbot run "Room Lead" "Rehearse the launch of https://example.com" --export ./out ``` See [Run OpenMausBot from scripts and CI](docs/headless-cli.md). ## Quick start **Released builds ([latest release](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/releases/latest)):** the harness server is embedded, so no separate server setup is required. | | Download | Install | |---|---|---| | **macOS** (Apple silicon) | [OpenMausBot.dmg](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/releases/latest/download/OpenMausBot.dmg) | Drag it to Applications, open it. Signed & notarized. | | **macOS** (Intel) | [OpenMausBot-intel.dmg](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/releases/latest/download/OpenMausBot-intel.dmg) | Same app, built for Intel Macs. Signed & notarized. | | **Windows** (x64) | [OpenMausBot-setup.exe](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/releases/latest/download/OpenMausBot-setup.exe) | Run it — one-click, per-user, no admin rights. The installer isn't code-signed yet, so SmartScreen shows "unknown publisher": **More info → Run anyway**. | | **Ubuntu 24.04** (x64) | [OpenMausBot-amd64.deb](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/releases/latest/download/OpenMausBot-amd64.deb) · [OpenMausBot.AppImage](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/releases/latest/download/OpenMausBot.AppImage) | Install the `.deb` with APT (recommended), or make the AppImage executable and run it. Beta; GNOME is the supported desktop. | See the [Ubuntu Desktop guide](docs/linux-desktop.md) for installation, capabilities, and troubleshooting. Any desktop build can also pair as a client to another Windows, macOS, or Ubuntu host over Tailscale; see [desktop-to-desktop companion mode](docs/desktop-companion.md). **From source:** ```sh git clone https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot && cd OpenMausBot pnpm install pnpm dev:server # harness server → 127.0.0.1:8799 pnpm dev # app → http://127.0.0.1:5199 pnpm dev:desktop # Electron shell; keep the two commands above running ``` Requirements: **macOS, Windows, or Ubuntu 24.04 x64**, **Node 24+**, **pnpm**, and at least one agent CLI — [`claude`](https://claude.com/claude-code), [`codex`](https://github.com/openai/codex), or [`grok`](https://x.ai/cli) — installed and logged in. They appear in the model picker automatically. Package the desktop application: ```sh pnpm package:mac # macOS: DMG + ZIP; requires Swift/Xcode tools pnpm package:win # Windows: installer + ZIP pnpm package:linux # Ubuntu x64: .deb + AppImage + verified CUA runtime ``` ### Desktop capability status | Capability | macOS | Ubuntu 24.04 Xorg | Ubuntu 24.04 Wayland | |---|---|---|---| | Packaged app, embedded harness, local agent CLIs | Supported | Beta | Beta | | Composio and Boat/cloud computers | Supported | Beta | Beta | | Explicit preview-only local screen capture | Supported | Beta | Beta | | Bot control of this computer | Supported | Beta, explicit opt-in | Disabled: Wayland safety gate | | Native on-device dictation | Supported | Planned | Planned | The Linux preview is user-initiated and never enables local bot control or Auto routing. On Xorg, the reviewed Cua Driver 0.19.3 runtime starts only after explicit opt-in and without its full-screen cursor overlay. On Wayland the app never starts it and clears legacy opt-ins while that real-seat safety gate remains unresolved. Chat, preview, Cloud, and Local VM remain available on both sessions. See the [Ubuntu Desktop guide](docs/linux-desktop.md) and tracking issues [#29](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/issues/29), [#345](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/issues/345), and [#113](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/issues/113). The Linux packager downloads only the tag-pinned upstream archive during the build, verifies its size, SHA-256, complete member allowlist, and inner executable hashes, then packages only the CLI and cursor-theme sidecar. The installed app never downloads or self-updates native automation code. Cua's MIT notice, Inter's SIL OFL, a generated third-party license report, and a CycloneDX inventory ship with the runtime. See [`third_party/cua-driver/`](third_party/cua-driver/) for the reviewed provenance record. These credentials are optional — local chat works without them. Paste a key once in **App Settings** (gear in the sidebar footer) when you want to enable its integration: | Credential | What it enables | Where to get it | |---|---|---| | Composio project key (`ak_…`) | Connect Gmail, GitHub, Slack, Notion, and other apps to your bots | [OpenMausBot Composio setup](docs/composio.md) | | Boat API key | Give bots an isolated remote Linux computer with a desktop and terminal | [Boat API key guide](https://docs.boat.dev/api-keys) | | ElevenLabs key | Read replies aloud, and call your bots | [ElevenLabs API keys](https://elevenlabs.io/app/settings/api-keys) | | Fish Audio key | Read replies aloud with Fish Audio voices, and call your bots | [Fish Audio API keys](https://fish.audio/app/api-keys/) | Composio and Boat are third-party services with their own accounts and terms. Boat is a paid service after its trial, and using a cloud computer may incur charges. ```sh pnpm typecheck # app + server pnpm test # unit, driver, API, and desktop capability tests pnpm build # typecheck + production build pnpm check:electron # syntax-check Electron main/preload files pnpm package:win # Windows installer + zip → release/ pnpm package:linux # Ubuntu x64 .deb + AppImage → release/ ``` ### Triggers: schedules and webhooks A trigger is "when something happens, a bot does something". Tell a bot "every weekday at 9, send me a summary of my inbox" or "whenever our form calls, draft a reply" and it sets the trigger up in that turn with its `trigger` tool (no confirmation; the chat shows a live card with Edit, Pause and Undo). **Triggers**, first in the sidebar, lists every schedule and webhook, with a calendar and the run history. Bots manage them with `trigger_info` (list, app events), `trigger` (create, update, pause, resume, run now) and `delete_trigger`; a webhook a bot makes never shows the bot its secret: the person copies the link from the card or the Triggers page. Schedules (routines) can run once, on selected weekdays, or every 5–1,440 minutes, using either a bot's configured model/computer or the Cloud VM runner. Interval schedules stay aligned to their chosen start time and skip an occurrence when the previous run is still active, so slow work cannot build an unbounded queue. A separate optional Advanced run limit can safely stop stuck work; no timeout is imposed unless one is chosen. The existing duration field remains calendar/display metadata. Webhook triggers are independent from schedules but reuse the same queued task executor and calendar receipts. **App events** start a bot when something happens in a connected app ("whenever I get an email from Acme, draft a reply"). The bot finds the app's events with `trigger_info` (`action: "events"`) and calls `trigger` with `action: "create"` and `when: "app_event"`; the person can also choose **New → Set it up yourself → When something happens in an app**. Composio sends each event to OpenMausBot's connected-apps service, which queues it; the app collects the queue with a long poll, so a desktop needs no public address and events wait while it is closed. Gmail is checked every 15 minutes; Slack, GitHub and other push apps arrive at once. A desktop keeps up to 500 events a day and a paid Cloud 2,000; what is skipped shows on the automation. App events need the included connected apps: a server using its own Composio key cannot watch apps yet. Details: [docs/composio.md](docs/composio.md#app-events). OpenMausBot starts a webhook-only receiver on `127.0.0.1:8800` by default (or one port above `OMB_PORT`). Set `OMB_WEBHOOK_PORT` to choose another port. A webhook secret is shown once when the trigger is created or rotated. Bearer authentication is recommended so the secret stays out of request URLs and most access logs; a single capability URL remains available for senders that cannot configure headers. The receiver exposes only `/health` and secret `/hooks/...` endpoints; it never exposes the app's broader API. OpenMausBot must remain running to accept a delivery. For public internet delivery, proxy only this dedicated receiver through a hosted relay or a tool such as Tailscale Funnel. ## Status Early but real — the loop works end to end: message → agent → streamed reply → tools → approvals → computer use. macOS, Windows, and Ubuntu 24.04 x64 have released builds; Ubuntu remains a beta with the capability limits above. Rough edges to expect: hosted/mobile connectivity is still being built, and webhook triggers currently use the local receiver rather than an always-on hosted relay. Hosted voice needs an ElevenLabs, Fish Audio, or xAI key; built-in Mac and local Chatterbox voices need no cloud key. Calls are macOS-only for now (they ride the same on-device dictation as the composer mic) — see [`docs/voice-mode.md`](docs/voice-mode.md) for the design and the known gaps. Contributions welcome — the driver SPI in [`server/contracts.ts`](server/contracts.ts) is deliberately small; adding a provider is one file in [`server/drivers/`](server/drivers/) plus a one-line registration. No code needed at all for your own engines: any ACP-speaking CLI or OpenAI-compatible endpoint plugs in through config — see [`docs/custom-engines.md`](docs/custom-engines.md). Users can add their own MCP tool servers with zero code via [`docs/custom-mcp-servers.md`](docs/custom-mcp-servers.md). To run bots on OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, DeepSeek, Cline or your own OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible provider, see [Other model providers](apps/docs/content/docs/providers/model-providers.mdx). ## Privacy Usage analytics are optional and anonymous: product events and a once-a-day count of what is set up, never keys, names, addresses or conversations. Turn them off in Settings → General → Usage analytics; [`docs/analytics.md`](docs/analytics.md) lists every event and property. ## Support the project OpenMausBot is free and open source. If it does real work for you, you can [support its development through GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/milind-soni) with a one-time contribution or a monthly sponsorship. Your support helps fund ongoing development and maintenance; OpenMausBot remains free and open source. ## Run from a terminal or on a server With Node 24 or newer, install once and run: ```sh npm install -g openmausbot openmausbot ``` Or use `npx openmausbot` without a global install. First launch guides you with arrow-key choices: choose AI access, sign in or paste a hidden API key, choose a model, and optionally connect a phone. Next time, the same command reuses your saved setup and opens OpenMausBot on this computer. Keep the terminal open; Ctrl-C stops the server, not your saved work. Use `--no-open` to skip opening the browser. Phone access is optional and defaults to skipping. Choose an explicitly approved managed public HTTPS endpoint protected by pairing, an existing Tailscale connection, or your own HTTPS reverse proxy. Both native apps pair from this flow: the QR is an app link when you are connecting an Android phone, and the iOS app takes either that or the web link. A browser works on either phone. A phone cannot use a localhost link. `--local` ignores saved remote access for one launch; `--no-pair` suppresses phone prompts and invitations but does not disable a saved remote connection. The web UI can also be installed from Safari or Chrome as a standalone phone app. See [Install the phone web app](docs/phone-web-app.md) for Home Screen installation and pairing. Run `openmausbot setup` to reconfigure without resetting bots or conversations; the saved model default applies only to new bots. Native setup confirms provider sign-in; API setup asks before a potentially billable test message. API keys are saved as plaintext, not encrypted, in private `config.json` (`0600` on Unix). See the [short setup guide](docs/cli-onboarding.md) for account differences, phone choices, credential storage, and cancellation. For a background service on a VPS or an always-on computer, use `npx openmausbot serve` with explicit remote options: `--tunnel` after `npx openmausbot login` for a managed public address, `--tailscale` for your tailnet, or the Docker stack for your own domain. These are separate from AI-provider sign-in. Devices pair once with a short code. The deployment guide is [docs/deploy-vps.md](docs/deploy-vps.md); the reference is [docs/self-hosting.md](docs/self-hosting.md). ## License [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE) © 2026 Milind Soni and OpenMausBot contributors, except `enterprise/`, which is source-available under its [own license](enterprise/LICENSE); delete that folder and what remains is the open-source edition. Details, including how contributions are signed off, are in [LICENSING.md](LICENSING.md). Packaged Cua Driver components retain their upstream MIT, SIL OFL 1.1, MPL-2.0, and other dependency terms; the corresponding notices, license texts, source locations, and SBOM are in [`third_party/cua-driver/`](third_party/cua-driver/) and ship beside the native runtime. OpenMausBot is an independent, open-source project inspired by Grok Bot. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or associated with xAI; "Grok" is a trademark of its respective owner.

The federated code forge · The Tangled Blog                                                The federated code forge              Anirudh   30 October 2026      For most of the past two decades, the code forge has been where projects live:
where code is hosted, where changes are reviewed, and where contributors find
each other. Forges offered convenience in exchange for centralisation. 
 But the centralised forge is crumbling. Relying on someone else for uptime, for
features, and to be a good steward of your code hasn’t played out well. What
 has  stood the test of time is email: Git to move the code, and email — an
open protocol — to talk about it. At the cost of user experience, however. 
          ’05      Mail   +   Git    ’09      GitHub   +   Git    ’25      AT Protocol   +   Git        
 Tangled aims to give you the best of both: the longevity of an open
protocol, with the convenience and polish of a proper forge. 
 It’s the first truly federated code forge — you can host code on your own
servers and still collaborate seamlessly with others. Our approach is
pragmatic: self-host just the parts you want, like Git hosting or CI runners,
or all of it, including the API server and UI. Whatever  you
choose , you can still talk to everyone
else. 
 Owning your infrastructure also means you can hack on, extend
and customise your forge as you see fit. Because Tangled is
built on the AT Protocol, you can build your own extensions,
subscribe to the firehose, or even write entirely custom knots,
like  this one  that runs on
Cloudflare Workers and uses their Artifacts product for git
storage. Or an entirely custom spindle such as
 mitchellh.com/tack . Go
even further and host our  ultralight API
server  and build
your own custom forge. 
 Agents have made building such hyper-personalized software trivial, and
especially so when software is designed with hackability in mind from the
get-go. Tangled is incredibly  agent 
 friendly . 
 The future of software engineering may be a moving target, but our bets
on open protocols and developer agency give us the agility to move with
it, and to become    y  o  u  r     c  o  d  e     f  o  r  g  e     f  o  r     t  h  e     n  e  x  t     d  e  c  a  d  e   . 
 Product updates 
 A fresh look! 
 The obvious big one: with this release, Tangled has a whole new look.
We’ve redone the UI on top of our new architecture (described further
below), in Svelte. Things should now be quicker, visually consistent and
prettier! The keen eyed of you might’ve also spotted that we’ve swapped
out Inter for  Timeless Sans . 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
 A bobbin near you 
 Until now, Tangled’s web UI and backend were a single Go monolith called the
 appview . The appview service handled AT Protocol indexing, caching,
off-protocol data and UI rendering using  html/template  + htmx. It ran on a
single SQLite database on one medium-sized server in Sweden. 
 This was great as long as you were ~50–100 ms away from Sweden,
but most of our users aren’t! We rearchitected: we built a new
standalone frontend app in Svelte, deployed at the edge. It is
populated by our new diskless, entirely in-memory indexer
service written in Rust:
 bobbin .
Bobbins are deployed globally in over 11+ regions, ensuring
users around the world get the best API and UI performance. 
 The astute reader might’ve noticed: bobbin is purely read-only and only
deals with AT Protocol data. What of the rest? That functionality (and
more) has been delegated to a new set of supporting services. 
 The new data model and repo-owned data 
 First, the data model itself: we have a new set of lexicons, and everything now
lives under  org.tangled.* , replacing the old  sh.tangled.*  records. 
 Knot2 is our aptly named, second implementation of the knot server, this time
rewritten in Rust. Knot2 bakes a fully custom Git server, and also bundles in
an SSH server in the same binary. 
 With knot2, we’ve also changed where some of that data lives. Issues, pull
requests, comments, reactions and labels are now stored on the knot, right next
to the code, as collaborative objects (COBs). A COB is just a chain of Git
objects in the repo itself. Collaborators, knot members and the blocklist are
also stored the same way. 
 In that sense, knots now behave a lot like a PDS: they hold signed records,
full history included, for everything that belongs to a repo and much like a
PDS, these records are synced via the standard AT Protocol firehose. 
 But why? A project’s issues and pull requests are as much a part of it as its code,
so they should live with it, wherever you choose to host it. This gives your
project maximum portability. 
 If the knot writes your issues and comments, what stops it from putting words
in your mouth? Attestations. Every time you create or edit a record on a knot,
the web app also writes an  org.tangled.graph.attestation  record to your own
PDS, pointing at that exact version of the record and the COB change behind it.
Two-way verification! 
                                                                                                                          
 Self-hosters will have to upgrade their knots to the v1.20.0 by  following the
upgrade guide . 
 Organizations 
 Organization accounts are here! An Organization on Tangled is a real AT
Protocol account, with its own DID and handle, hosted on a  Tranquil
PDS  instance. They’re
passwordless, delegated accounts: you create one from the  New
Organization  page, and you get
 <name>.tngl.sh  with yourself as its owner. Owners can invite members, and
anyone in the Organization can act as it when creating or forking repositories.
Like any other account, you can swap the handle out for a domain you own. If
you’ve been running a regular account as a stand-in “org”, hang tight — we’re
working on a way to move those over. Read more in the
 docs . 
                                                                                
 Stacked PRs for everyone 
 Our PR flow has been overhauled. The new flow gives everyone, regardless
of whether you use Jujutsu or just vanilla Git, the ability to submit
and review stacked PRs. If you’re using Git, you now get the ability to
interdiff between versions (previously called rounds). JJ users get to
interdiff between individual changes as well. 
                                                                                                              
 Launch weeks ahead 
 This isn’t all. We’re staggering this launch across the next few weeks. Up next
are private repos, a CLI, SDKs for different languages and skills for your
agent. 
 Until then, enjoy every part of this launch equally.          Your code, your network.  Come build with us on Tangled.           Sign up                                      © 2026 Tangled Labs Oy.   Tangled  Docs  Source  Brand  Discord  Bluesky  X/Twitter  Terms  Privacy

       Security update regarding one of our infrastructure providers 
       
            Incident

          Report for  bunny.net 
       
         Subscribe to Updates 
     

     
       

       
         
           
            Update
           
           
             
               We're providing an update on the reissuance of managed TLS certificates for custom domains.  Reissuance is ongoing and progressing steadily. To avoid any disruption to the delivery of your content, certificates are being reissued gradually in controlled batches, and each reissued certificate uses a new private key. This is taking longer than our initial estimate, and we now expect the process to be completed by the end of October 31. Your existing certificates continue to be served without interruption until they are replaced, and no action is required from customers using managed certificates.  If you manage your own TLS certificates, we continue to recommend revoking and reissuing them with new private keys as a precaution.  Neither our investigation nor the provider's ongoing investigation has found any new evidence of unauthorized access to our server. We'll post a further update on our status page once reissuance is complete.  If you have any questions or need help with managing your TLS certificates, our support team will be happy to assist. 
             
             
              Posted   Oct  29 ,  2026  -  18:40  UTC
             
           
         
         
           
            Monitoring
           
           
             
               We're reaching out to inform you of a security incident involving one of our infrastructure providers, the steps we've taken, and what this means for you.  - What happened and how we responded  Last week, one of our infrastructure providers reported unauthorized access involving third-party server management software. One of our CDN nodes, located in Armenia, was hosted on a server supplied by this provider.  After receiving the alert from the affected provider, our engineering team took immediate action. Within 20 minutes, we stopped routing traffic through the server. We then reviewed and preserved the relevant security logs for investigation, securely wiped the server, and revoked its access to our other systems. The affected server has been permanently removed from our infrastructure.  Our investigation found no evidence of unauthorized access to the CDN node or any of its data. The infrastructure provider has also found no evidence that our server was accessed, but continues to investigate the incident.  - What this means for your data  While neither investigation has found any indication of unauthorized access to our server, we cannot completely rule out the possibility.  If unauthorized access to our CDN node did occur, the potentially exposed information would have been: temporarily cached CDN content, Pull Zone configurations, and TLS certificates stored on that server.  As an additional precaution, we have revoked and reissued all TLS certificates for bunny.﻿net platform domains (b-cdn.﻿net and bunny.﻿run). Reissuance of managed TLS certificates for custom domains is ongoing and is expected to be completed within the next 24 hours. No action is required from customers using managed certificates. We will post a further update on our status page once this process is complete.  If you manage your own TLS certificates, we recommend revoking and reissuing them with new private keys as a precaution.  No other customer data, including bunny.﻿net account data, was stored on the server in question, and no internal systems were affected.  - What happens next  We’re closely monitoring our infrastructure and working with the affected provider as the investigation continues. Should any new findings affect our customers, we will provide an update via email and on our status page.  At bunny.﻿net, we understand the trust you place in us to keep your content secure, and we take that responsibility seriously. If you have any questions or need help with managing your TLS certificates, our support team will be happy to assist.

                        Observability Real Talk                   Subscribe  Sign in                    AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them.  When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters?                        Elizabeth      Feb 28, 2026              17        3     3      Share               💌   Hey there, it’s Elizabeth from SigNoz!    This newsletter is   a   n honest attempt to talk about all things - observability, OpenTelemetry, open-source and the engineering in between!    &   This piece took 6 days, 5 hours to be cooked, hope we served.    🌚                         Subscribe                 There are two popular prophecies floating around tech circles these days.   The first says    SRE is the future of all software engineering   , that as AI writes more and more code, the humans who remain will be the ones keeping systems alive. The second says AI will devour every tech job alive, SREs included. Neither is particularly useful if you’re an SRE trying to figure out what your Tuesday will look like in 2027.   Let’s ask a more grounded question by looking at what’s already happening: When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters?                          Most of us already use AI for our daily work (our brains a little fried!), and so do SREs. Today’s discussion agenda is not whether AI replaces SREs, but whether AI is quietly making SREs less capable and whether anyone will notice anything before the next novel outage hits. The foundational framework for this entire debate comes from a 1983 research paper that’s eerily prescient.    The Ironies of Automation: Part-I              Note from author: Below is a brief precursor to History of Automation, which you might enjoy if you are into History and Cultures (like me 😉).      In 1983, a cognitive psychologist named Lisanne Bainbridge published a paper called     Ironies of Automation    . It became one of the most cited papers in human factors research, and its core argument is almost uncomfortably relevant today.   Bainbridge studied what happened when factories and industrial systems automated the work of blue-collar operators. The findings were paradoxical and revealed that the more you automate a process, the more critical the human operator becomes during the rare moments automation fails and the less practice they get, and the worse they become at exactly those interventions. Automation, which was inherently designed to remove humans from the loop, left them with the worst possible job, i.e., long stretches of passive monitoring punctuated by rare, high-stakes crises they were increasingly unprepared for.  Ring any bells yet? 🙂  Basically, I’m drawing a parallel between the AI revolution and industrial automation. Industrial automation reshaped blue-collar work by taking over routine physical tasks, and the workers who remained had to handle exceptions they’d lost the muscle memory for. AI is doing the same thing to knowledge workers by taking over the routine cognitive tasks, the pattern matching, the triage, the known-issue resolution and leaving humans with the rare, complex, ambiguous problems.   The   exact   problems that require deep   expertise  , the   exact expertise   that atrophies when you stop practising.   Now we’re replaying this pattern with AI agents, and the stakes in software systems are only growing.    Current State of AI in SRE           Let’s take stock of where things stand today in the world of site reliability engineering.   What’s already automated or heavily AI-assisted?            Alert noise reduction and intelligent grouping, runbook execution for known issues, log pattern detection and anomaly flagging, and basic root-cause suggestions from historical incident data, and auto-remediation for well-understood failure modes like restarting a crashed pod or scaling up a service that’s running hot, are all fairly automated today.     What’s on the horizon?            Some immediate targets include multi-signal correlation across metrics, logs, and traces, autonomous root-cause analysis for partially understood failures, predictive incident detection before users are affected, AI-driven change risk assessment and automated rollbacks.  PagerDuty frames this as a tiered model.    Tier 1 incidents: Known issues with known fixes get fully automated.    Tier 2 incidents: Partially understood problems receive AI recommendations with human validation.    Tier 3 incidents: Novel, complex, cascading failures stay human-led, with AI providing supporting context.    But here’s the catch.   If   human   SREs (okay, now we have to use adjectives like human 🥹) only engage with Tier 3 incidents, i.e. the novel, never-before-seen outages, where do they build the   intuition   to handle them? Intuition is usually developed from years of hands-on incident response, pattern recognition built through repetition, and the kind of gut-level understanding of a system that only develops from painfully waking up at the odd hour to solve the bug that brought the system down.        Subscribe if you wish to read some more hot takes. We are cooking some great ones!                         Subscribe              The Crisis of Deskilling           This is where the picture starts getting blurry. Let’s look at some emerging research on AI-induced deskilling across multiple fields, which paints a consistent and concerning picture.   In medicine, a   recent study   found that endoscopists who used AI assistance for polyp detection saw their unassisted detection rates drop from 28% to 22% after a period of AI use. They got worse at the thing they were supposed to be experts in, not because they forgot the theory, but because they stopped exercising the skill.    In aviation,   research   has shown that long-haul pilots who rely heavily on autopilot systems experience measurable degradation in situational awareness and manual flying ability. The problem got serious enough that the FAA now mandates more manual flying time to counteract the effect.    Somewhere over the past year, AI stopped being a tool I occasionally reached for and became the first thing I reach for,   always  . My instinct now is to offload as much as possible and apply my own thinking only where it’s absolutely unavoidable. The problem is that these moments are becoming the only exercises my brain gets, and I can feel the   rust  .    We can draw a pattern here. The more you let the system handle, the worse you get at handling things yourself and here’s the truly dangerous part,   you don’t feel it happening  . It gets masked as hyper-productivity. Cognitive research suggests that because AI tools make tasks feel easier and enhance visible performance, users are often unable to accurately judge the true status of their own skills. You feel competent, dashboards look green, and then on a Wednesday, a novel incident hits that doesn’t match any pattern the AI has seen, and you realise the muscle has atrophied.   For SREs, this manifests in specific ways, like we stop reading raw log streams because the AI summarises them, we stop forming hypotheses during incidents because the AI suggests root causes, we stop building mental models of system architecture because the AI maps dependencies for us, and each of these individually looks like a productivity win. Collectively, they hollow out the very expertise that makes an SRE effective when things go sideways in ways nobody anticipated.   But there’s something even more concerning than deskilling, and researchers have started calling it   never-skilling  . Deskilling means you once had a capability but have since lost it. Never-skilling means you never developed it in the first place. For junior SREs entering the field today in an environment where AI handles most of the incident response workflow, the opportunities to build foundational intuition and muscle through hands-on practice are vanishing.    The training pipeline itself is broken and not   self-healing  .   SREs realise their skills are degrading and lean more on AI to compensate, which further degrades their skills, creating a vicious cycle from which escape is difficult.  What Can We Do About It?           We are definitely not rejecting AI tooling; we are adopting it and integrating it stronger than ever before, because that’s the only way forward.  A few approaches worth considering:   Deliberate inefficiency.   Just as the FAA mandates manual flying time even when the autopilot is perfectly capable, SRE teams can designate certain incidents, even the ones the AI could handle, as   human-practice opportunities  . This can be considered as a long-term investment to keep skills fresh, although it might come at the cost of a super-fast solution    Build for human-in-the-loop, not human-on-the-side.   There’s a meaningful difference between a system where a human approves an AI’s recommendation and one where a human actively engages with the problem alongside AI. The former keeps humans in a supervisory role that Bainbridge (the lady who wrote   that   research paper about 40 years ago) showed leads to vigilance decay, and the latter keeps them cognitively engaged.   Let’s zoom out and take a look at the bigger picture.  The Bigger Picture           Everything we’ve discussed here, the ironies of automation, the deskilling risk, the never-skilling problem, collectively applies well beyond SRE. Software engineering as a whole is navigating the same tension. As AI writes more code, reviews more PRs, and handles more debugging, the same questions apply.   We’re talking about SREs specifically because that’s the world we live in at    SigNoz   . We build an open-source observability platform, the kind of tool that gives SREs the metrics, traces, and logs they need to understand their systems deeply. For us, this deskilling question is not a rhetorical fad; it directly shapes how we’re building AI into our product.   Our approach is to start with an AI assistant that helps SREs leverage the power of LLMs while keeping humans firmly in control. Eventually, we’ll enable more autonomy but within clear guardrails, and only as trust is earned.  One advantage we have in this space is that, as an observability platform, we sit on the data itself, the metrics, traces, and logs that SREs rely on. Most AI SRE products today integrate with observability tools through APIs, which means they’re working with a limited, second-hand view of your systems. Because we own the data layer, we can build much deeper, more context-aware AI capabilities that understand your system the way an experienced SRE would.  And to answer the burning question in your head, our goal isn’t AI that replaces SREs. It’s AI that supercharges SREs. Unlike ongoing lore, we believe humans will remain essential for the decisions that matter most, especially those that impact production infrastructure.   The future of SRE is human   with   AI intentionally designed to keep humans sharp, engaged, and ready for the 5% that really counts. Eg I’ve seen a lot of Postgres-on-k8s solutions that are basically just Postgres on bare metal with a bunch of useless abstractions. It writes to local disk, moving the pod to a new host is basically restoring from backup. Wrap it in some tool that ingests YAML and call it a day. k8s is sort of the king of this. I hear people say they understand k8s and I can’t help but furrow my eyebrows. I don’t even pretend to, there are so many insanely complicated edge cases. Eg if I’m sending UDP packets to a service and scale the deployment from 2 pods to 4 and the host for one of the new pods crashes and comes back up with a bad iptables rule, what are the range of potential behaviors k8s would show?   Deskilling is good, actually, as long as it's the right deskilling. "Skill" in software development is partly raw IQ and partly knowledge of complexity. Programming author Fred Brooks (author of The Mythical Man-Month) categorized complexity into "essential" and "incidental". Examples of incidental complexity are: React/Rails/Django/Laravel makes a backward-incompatible change to their interface and you need to scurry around the codebase fixing invocations. Or a senior developers on your team have a weird in-house coding style and all the junior devs need to learn it to get their code approved. Or management wants to move everything from one cloud provider to another so you have to change a bunch of resource URLs. Examples of essential complexity are: Self-driving car algorithms. Making your code run faster on the CPU. Adding support for a new web standard like SPDY. I'm not lamenting the days when you needed to pull a seasoned (read: exquisitely expensive) COVOL developer out of retirement to make a change. Now AI can figure it out well enough, I just need to know how the basic concepts work.      reply                             hsuduebc2    3 hours ago       |  prev  |  next   [–]

--- license: mit library_name: transformers pipeline_tag: image-text-to-text --- # DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017

Technical Report 👁️

## Introduction **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017** is a minor update to [**DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash**](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash), delivering substantial improvements across reasoning, coding, agentic tasks, and visual benchmarks. Alongside these gains, the model reduces task execution time and output length, enabling users to complete tasks faster and at lower cost and advancing the performance–cost Pareto frontier across multiple agent harnesses.
| Benchmark | DS-V4.1-Flash-1017 | DS-V4.1-Flash | K3 | GLM-5.3 | GPT-5.6 Sol | Opus 5 | | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | HLE w/o tools | 42.6 (44.0†) | 36.8 (39.1†) | 43.5 | 42.0† | 44.5 | 56.3 | | Terminal-Bench 4.0 | 42.3 | 31.2 | 12.6 | 37.9 | 39.9 | 51.8 | | DeepSWE v1.1 | 77.0 | 74.2 | 67.5 | 66.9 | 73.0 | 74.0 | | ProgramBench | 29.1 | 20.3 | 17.5 | 19.0 | 23.0 | 37.0 | | NL2Repo-Bench | 68.2 | 65.4 | 58.0 | 58.0 | 56.8 | 75.3 | | Automation-Bench v1.0.6 | 60.5 | 54.8 | 46.7 | 48.8 | 45.8 | 50.3 | | Agents’ Last Exam | 35.4 | 31.8 | 27.6 | 28.5 | 26.7 | 28.6 | | Apex Bench v1.1 | 72.1 | 64.6 | 47.8 | 56.6 | 54.3 | 65.8 | | Chartography (w/tools) | 83.0 | 78.9 | 68.1 | — | 79.9 | 84.0 | | BabyVision (w/tools) | 92.5 | 89.6 | 85.7 | — | 88.9 | 94.1 | | ZeroBench-main (w/tools) | 51.0 | 49.0 | 41.0 | — | 53.0 | 52.0 |
*† denotes the text-only subset of HLE. We use the Claude Code harness for Terminal-Bench 4.0 and the Mini-SWE-V2 harness for DeepSWE v1.1.* ## Prompt Encoding This release does not include a Jinja-format chat template. The [`encoding`](encoding/README.md) folder contains a self-contained Python reference implementation (`encoding.py`) with test cases for multi-turn conversations, tool calling, thinking mode, numeric reasoning effort, mid-conversation system messages, and interleaved image content. For production use, we additionally release [deepseek-recipe](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-recipe), a set of Rust libraries with Python bindings that provides the same prompt format as a maintained, protocol-aware toolkit. It converts Messages, Chat Completions, and Responses API requests into the Conversation format, encodes them into DeepSeek V4 and V4.1 prompts or token IDs, and parses model output back into complete or streamed responses — covering thinking, tool calls, images, and generation settings. Model inference, tool execution, and HTTP transport are left to the caller. ## Minimal Inference Please refer to the [`inference`](inference/README.md) folder for instructions on weight conversion and running inference locally. **Recommended sampling parameters:** | Parameter | Value | | :--- | :--- | | `temperature` | 1.0 | | `top_p` | 1.0 | | `context_window` | 1M tokens | | `max_tokens` | ≥ 256K | ## License This repository and the model weights are licensed under the [MIT License](LICENSE). ## Citation ```bibtex @misc{deepseekai2026deepseekv41flash, title={DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression}, author={DeepSeek-AI}, year={2026}, } ``` ## Contact If you have any questions, please raise an issue or contact us at [service@deepseek.com](mailto:service@deepseek.com).

Become a sponsor

**Taste Skill** is an Agent Skill that makes coding agents design websites and app screens instead of assembling the average landing page. It gives the agent an art direction, real pictures and a way to check its own work in a real browser. Pages it has built, each from one brief:
The photographs are real, found in open archives and credited by the skill ([credits](examples/v2/CREDITS.md)). Watch the [launch film](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill/releases/tag/v2.0.0). ## Install ```bash npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill --skill "design-taste-frontend" ``` That installs the skill with the [`npx skills`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills) CLI. The skill runs its scripts with **Node 22+** and an installed **Chrome, Edge or Chromium**. It installs nothing and needs no API keys. Finding pictures needs network access.
Claude Code plugin Run these inside Claude Code. The skill is namespaced under `taste-skill:`, so it does not collide with your other skills. ``` /plugin marketplace add Leonxlnx/taste-skill /plugin install taste-skill@taste-skill ``` `/plugin update` upgrades it later.
Codex plugin ```bash codex plugin marketplace add Leonxlnx/taste-skill codex plugin add taste-skill@taste-skill ``` Start a new Codex session afterwards so the skill is loaded.
From a clone, linked instead of copied `./install.sh` symlinks the skill into Claude Code (`--codex` for Codex, `--all-agents` for both), so a `git pull` updates it in place.
Already have the skill? Run the install command again; the install name did not change. Looking for one of the older skills? See [Moved skills](#moved-skills). ## How v2 works The skill is built from a study of 247 curated sites. A build runs in six steps: 1. Reads the brief and lists what only this client has. 2. A script deals three of 20 researched directions and the agent picks one. 3. Finds the idea: one sentence tying the client's own material to that direction. 4. Builds with real pictures and footage from open collections, credited. 5. Checks the page in a real browser at three widths and fails it on slop. 6. Looks at its own screenshots and fixes the top three problems, up to three rounds. A build takes roughly 30 to 45 minutes and a few hundred thousand tokens. Details are in the [changelog](CHANGELOG.md) and the [study](skills/taste-skill/references/research.md). Dashboards and app screens (v2.1) take their own route: the skill deals one of the app styles distilled from real product screens, builds the shell, the data, the charts and the tables to those numbers, and checks the result with app rules: quiet panels, aligned figures, colour spent on data, a phone layout where the navigation folds away. A product's landing page builds the app it shows the same way, so its screenshots look like a working product. v2.1 also checks the frame of every page (a clear title on the first screen, equal margins, no section shoved to one side, no random blank stretches) and moves the way strong award sites do, measured on the latest 100 Awwwards Sites of the Day. ## Moved skills This repo holds one skill, `design-taste-frontend`. The others moved to repos of their own and kept their install names: | Install name | Where it lives now | | --- | --- | | `high-end-visual-design`, `minimalist-ui`, `industrial-brutalist-ui`, `gpt-taste`, `stitch-design-taste`, `design-taste-frontend-v1`, `design-taste-frontend-v2-experimental` | **[Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics)** | | `imagegen-frontend-web`, `imagegen-frontend-mobile`, `brandkit`, `image-to-code` | **[Leonxlnx/imagegen-skills](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/imagegen-skills)** | | `redesign-existing-projects` | Part of `design-taste-frontend`, which audits an existing page in a real browser before changing anything | | `full-output-enforcement` | Removed. For the same problem, see **[Leonxlnx/unlazy](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/unlazy)** | Install a moved skill from its new repo under the same name: ```bash npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics --skill "high-end-visual-design" ``` ## Common Questions **What does the skill need?** Node 22 or newer and Chrome, Edge or Chromium. It installs nothing and uses no API keys. It needs the internet only to find pictures. **Where do the pictures come from, and can I use them?** From open collections such as Wikimedia Commons, Openverse and the Met. Only public domain, CC0, CC BY and CC BY-SA files are offered, and the skill puts the credits on the page. Replace them with your own when you have them. **Does it work with React, Vue, Svelte, plain HTML?** Yes. The rules are about design, not a framework. **Is it for dashboards and app screens?** Yes, since v2.1. The skill tells a page from an app screen and builds a dashboard, an admin view or a settings screen with its own run: a style dealt from a study of real product screens, quiet panels, honest data and charts, and its own checks (`inspect.mjs --app`). ## Support the project If Taste Skill helps you, consider sponsoring: [Sponsor on GitHub](https://github.com/sponsors/Leonxlnx) ### Open Source Supporters

Get a Kimi API key: taste-skill users get 10% bonus API credits on their first purchase.
### Community Sponsors

Feedback: open an issue or pull request, DM [@lexnlin](https://x.com/lexnlin) or [@blueemi99](https://x.com/blueemi99), or email [hello@tasteskill.dev](mailto:hello@tasteskill.dev). Taste Skill has no official token, coin, or crypto project. Any token using my name, image, or project is unaffiliated and not endorsed by me. ## License [MIT License](LICENSE) · Copyright (c) 2026 Leonxlnx

> ***NOTE***: If you came here from Hacker News, (1) yes this is all vibe-coded; (2) a more readable description of the project can be found here: https://github.com/emmilco/us-tax-model/blob/main/spec/spec.md


# us-tax-model

The forms-and-instructions layer of US federal individual income tax as public, cited, machine-checkable
data, with a guided self-preparation interview as its first client. The interview asks a person
questions, decides which forms apply, computes them, explains every value and hands back a values sheet
the person files themselves. The software never files, signs or transmits a return, and no return data
leaves the machine. What is encoded is the IRS's published procedure, not the Internal Revenue Code.

## Why you can check it

The encoding was written largely by language-model agents, so it cannot be trusted because of who wrote
it; it is built so that what matters can be checked from the repository alone by someone who trusts none
of the authors. Each layer states what it is, what it guarantees, what it does not, and where to look.

### 1. Forms as data, with a citation on every line

Each form or worksheet is a YAML file under `forms/<year>/`. A line is a record: id, printed line number,
IRS label, type, one expression, and a citation naming the document, tax year, revision, locator and the
hash of the archived page under `sources/<year>/` it was read from (`spec/spec.md` section 5).
Guarantees: the build fails if any line, parameter, gate or question lacks a citation or cites a hash
absent from the manifest, and `tools/citations.py` verifies every quote and locator against the archived
text; `reports/2025/citations.md` reports 2,313 anchors and 1,252 quotes, 0 findings without a recorded
ruling, and 305 computed-line locator segments too coarse to verify. Does not guarantee: that the
expression says what the cited page says. A citation proves a line points at a page, not that it was read
correctly.

### 2. A closed atom vocabulary

Every computed line is one application of one atom from the list in `spec/spec.md` section 4.2 (`sum`,
`subtract_floor0`, `smaller_of`, `multiply_rate`, `round`, `table_lookup`, `choose` and a dozen others);
there are no user-defined functions, loops, variables, strings or recursion. Guarantees: the whole
meaning of the data is the meaning of about twenty operations, each small enough to read; the one escape,
`opaque`, a host-language function, is counted and published, and `reports/2025/coverage.md` reports 0 of
2,384 lines use it. Does not guarantee: that the right atom was chosen for a line.

### 3. The build-time checker

`engine/src/check.ts` fails the build unless every `copy`, operand and `param` reference resolves within
the stated revision; the line graph is acyclic; every expression type-checks (cents, rates, counts and
booleans do not mix); every `choose` has exhaustive and disjoint guards, decided by enumeration and
interval analysis; and the provenance rules of layer 1 hold (`spec/design.md` section 2.3). Guarantees:
no dangling reference, cycle, unit confusion, or gap or overlap in a guarded alternative anywhere in the
data. Does not guarantee: agreement with the IRS text; a wrong operand that type-checks passes.

### 4. The renderer

Each atom has one English template in IRS worksheet phrasing, and the renderer writes every line's
English beside the IRS label and the citation into `rendered/<year>/`, which is committed. Guarantees: a
non-programmer can read any line against the printed form, and a change to the data appears in review as
a readable English diff. Does not guarantee: that anyone has done that reading.

### 5. Integer arithmetic

Money is integer cents, rates are integer pairs, and the evaluator (`engine/`, `BigInt`) has no floating
point. Rounding happens only in the `round` atom, only where a cited instruction says to round, by the
rule it states (`spec/spec.md` section 3, item 10). Guarantees: every value is exact and every rounding
is cited. Does not guarantee: that the IRS meant its arithmetic to be exact; where the text leaves
rounding open, the reading chosen is in `ambiguities/<year>.yaml`.

### 6. Lean

`lean/TaxFormalization/` defines every atom over the integers (`Atoms.lean`), proves the properties of
`spec/spec.md` section 6.3 (`Lemmas.lean`: `subtractFloor0_nonneg`, `roundHalfUpToUnit_idem`,
`prorate_le_amount`), and has a reference evaluator over the same canonical JSON as the TypeScript one,
proved to terminate and to be deterministic (`EvalProps.lean`). Both evaluators run over every fixture
and generated return; `reports/2025/evaluator_agreement.md` reports 1,648 cases, 2,895,826 line values
compared, 0 differences. Guarantees: the atoms behave as specified, and two independently written
evaluators of the same data compute the same values. Does not guarantee: anything about whether the data
matches the IRS text. Both evaluators read the same files, so agreement shows the evaluators agree, not
that the data is right. `BUG_INVENTORY.md` entry BUG-0001 is the canonical case: Form 1040 line 9 summed
line 3a as well as 3b; every fixture and both evaluators agreed with the wrong sum; an outside engine
caught it.

### 7. Independent constructions

No comprehensive human line-by-line reading is claimed, so the project supplements optional readings with constructions that share
nothing but the archived pages (`spec/spec.md` section 6.5): a second transcription of each worksheet by
an isolated model given only the pages and the schema, compared atom by atom with the project's; a render
comparison, in which an isolated model that has not seen the YAML reads each line's English against the
page; class M hand-work, in which an isolated model works branch-covering inputs on the printed
worksheet; and blind predictions of whole-return values made before the encoding was run. Each model runs
with no repository access and no network (`tools/transcription/README.md`); every disagreement is ruled
against the source with the page and quote recorded, and the logs are committed under `reviews/2025/`.
Guarantees: for each line, two readings of the same page produced the same structure, or the difference
is on record with its ruling. Does not guarantee: independence of the readers.

### 8. Engines

`tools/engines/` generates whole returns and runs them through three engines, PolicyEngine-US 2.49.4,
Tax-Calculator 6.8.5 and OpenTaxSolver 23.06, comparing line for line where the engine computes a line;
`reports/2025/engine_differential.md` covers 1,700 returns. Every difference must be explained to a cited
cause or the run fails; a margin is never accepted, and the current report lists no unexplained
difference. The line-level OpenTaxSolver adapter is in use; UsTaxes remains to be added under
`docs/2026-10-22_integrity_plan.md`. Guarantees: the summary lines the engines reach agree with code
written by other people from the rules. Does not guarantee: anything about worksheet lines the engines do
not compute; the first two primarily reach summary lines, while OpenTaxSolver also reaches worksheet lines.

### 9. The evidence report and the scoreboard

`reports/2025/evidence.md` lists every line with the classes of evidence that assert it (A, an official
IRS example; B, human hand-work; C, a named outside calculator; M, isolated model hand-work; H, human source reading; E, an
engine; R, the project's own regression; `spec/spec.md` section 6.1). Its first line is the scoreboard,
the share of computed lines with at least one assertion from outside the Claude model family. The
2026-10-24 regenerated report reads 198 of 1,515 (13.1%); H: 0, B: 0, second-family M: 44, E: 163
(the sub-counts overlap). This reflects the recorded numeric assertions after the skipped-response
audit; it does not establish complete form or whole-return coverage. Form2441's three missing STOP
outputs remain uncredited and its form-level review remains pending. Optional human findings no
longer prevent report generation. This report refresh is not a new full-suite pass. Guarantees: the evidence behind any line can
be looked up, and the one number the project is moving is printed first. H credits a source reading
with a current receipt and the exact log committed by its named reader; it supplies no worked values
and never fills B. The owner completed the first packet; original findings are preserved and current
H credit remains zero. Further human packets and ruling samples are optional under the
[2026-10-24 policy amendment](docs/2026-10-24_validation_policy.md). Does not guarantee: that a line
with only A, Claude-family M or R assertions has been checked by anyone but one model family.

### 10. Mutation testing, properties, interview checks

The mutation tool applies single-atom mutations to the data (swap `smaller_of` for `larger_of`, drop a
floor, change an operand) and asks whether the checker or a fixture notices; `reports/2025/mutation.md`
reports 2,278 mutants, 128 surviving, each with a written proof of equivalence, so 94.4% raw and 100.0%
with equivalents excluded. Property tests check the data-level properties of spec 6.3 over 400 generated
returns; `reports/2025/properties.md` reports 8 properties, all holding. The interview's finite path
checks (`engine/`, `spec/spec.md` section 6.4) enumerate answer combinations: every path ends in a
complete form set or a cited refusal, answer order does not change the return, and no question is asked
whose answer cannot reach a line. Guarantees: the fixtures are sensitive to the data they claim to test,
the stated invariants hold, and the interview has no dead ends. Does not guarantee: anything a mutation
cannot express or a fixture already encodes wrongly (BUG-0001 again).

### 11. The bug inventory and the commit guard

`BUG_INVENTORY.md` records every defect caught by any check or reading, before or with its fix: how it
was caught, the symptom, the root cause, why the existing checks missed it, the fix and its commit. It is
append-only; `check-all` fails if the committed prefix changes or the ids are not sequential.
`tools/hooks/pre-commit` refuses any commit whose tree is not the tree the last green `npm run check-all`
tested, and a run is green only if nothing outside its own outputs changed while it ran
(`tools/README.md`, "Commit guard"). Guarantees: the defect record cannot be edited, and no commit lands
without the whole suite having passed on that exact tree. Does not guarantee: that the suite catches what
it does not test for; the "why it survived" field exists to turn each such miss into a new check.

## What this does not establish

From `spec/spec.md` section 3, item 11: *human source-reading coverage is limited to the per-line
evidence records; independent constructions and their recorded disagreements provide the broader
verification.* The report identifies qualifying outside-family assertions and the source of each.
Unfinished verification is reported as a gap; adopting the requirement does not establish its completion.

The original layer-7 constructions used one model family, Claude. Flash has now completed transcription
and render calls over all 55 forms and worked six active Form 2441 cases and one W-2 return. Many
source disagreements and three blank numeric outputs after a Form2441 STOP remain; the second
family has not been promoted. The regenerated scoreboard credits 198 computed lines across the
recorded engine and second-family worked-value assertions; complete-form coverage remains separate.
Current source-reading eligibility is in `reports/2025/second_family.md`. Transcription/render readings are
subject to their individual gates. BUG-0129 exposed unit erasure in the transcription comparer;
transcription qualification is held until that defect and prior agreements are audited. Model worked
values and external-engine assertions are separate from this hold. Source readings are
reported separately and are not yet wired into the scoreboard. The amended integrity plan strengthens
second-family and engine checks, with human readings optional. Online tax interpretation is recorded
as non-authoritative corroboration under `research/secondary/`; it earns no scoreboard credit and
stays separate from blind source-only model requests.

The IRS forms and instructions are not the law. They embed judgments about the Internal Revenue Code that
are not announced, and this project encodes the published procedure, judgments included; where the text
is ambiguous or silent, the reading chosen is recorded in `ambiguities/<year>.yaml` and shown to the user
when it affects their return. No lawyer has reviewed the legal position the project operates under
(`spec/spec.md` section 9).

## Scope and coverage

The forms and lines computed are listed in `spec/spec.md` section 2.1, the situations refused with a
cited explanation in section 2.2, and the order of the remaining additions in section 2.4; the tool never
refuses silently. Coverage is measured over whole returns (a return counts only when nothing on it is
refused) by `tools/coverage/estimate.py` into `reports/2025/filer_coverage.md`, which today reads 68.6%
of individual returns. Its caveat: 148 of the 157 refusal gates are not measured (no IRS count or
microdata variable), so the figure is of the measured situations only and the true coverage is lower by
the unmeasured gates' share.

## How to run everything

One command rebuilds the data, runs every check and records the tested tree:

```sh
npm install
npm run check-all
```

Prerequisites, as inspected when the toolchain was first checked (`tools/README.md`, "Toolchain
inspected"): Node and npm; Lean 4 through elan (`lean/lean-toolchain` pins the version) with Lake;
Poppler's `pdftotext`; Python 3 with PyYAML; curl; and, for the extraction check's PDFKit reading of the
PDFs (`tools/extraction/pdfkit_text.swift`), macOS with the Swift toolchain. The check runs offline on a
fresh clone. The engine differential (`tools/engines/README.md`) needs the two outside engines installed
with `tools/engines/setup.sh`, the one network step; without them that step skips visibly and the check
is not claimed. The commit guard is a git hook, enabled with `git config core.hooksPath tools/hooks`.

## Standing notices

Shown at first run and on every output (`spec/spec.md` section 8):

- This is not tax or legal advice.
- The user is responsible for the return.
- The tool implements published IRS forms and instructions, which are not the law itself.
- It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the IRS.
- The list of what it covers and does not cover (above).

## Where things are

`PROJECT_INDEX.md` lists every directory, what it holds and the naming conventions. `HANDOFF.md` and the
current `HANDOFF-STAGE-*.md` are the reading order for a session continuing the build.

## Licences

Code is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 (`LICENSE`). The data is dedicated to the public
domain under CC0 1.0 Universal (`LICENSE-DATA`): `forms/`, `params/`, `tables/`, `fixtures/`,
`ambiguities/` and `interview/`. The archived IRS sources under `sources/` are IRS publications.
